title: CRITICAL: every JSX-based dashboard page rendered '[object Object]' instead of content
description:
Found and fixed 2026-09-03 while building the bindings dashboard UI (archie-core-t2db.8), via real browser verification per AGENTS.md's UI rule -- not caught by any existing test, since unit tests render components in isolation via @testing-library/preact and never exercise the actual router/mount integration path.

Every page registered in ui/src/main.jsx's routes table (dashboard, tasks, logs, captures, mappings, skills, workflows, memory, curators, channels, settings) returns a Preact VNode from its page function (e.g. dashboardPage() returns <DashboardApp />), but main.jsx's router passed that VNode into ui/src/base/dom.jsx's mount()/append(), which only knows how to append real DOM Nodes or String()-ify everything else -- so every page's actual content became the literal text "[object Object]" in the browser. Confirmed via git show that this bug already existed in the committed ui/dist bundle before any change tonight -- served the pre-existing bundle in isolation via a throwaway webui.Server harness and reproduced the identical failure on the stock dashboard. This shipped in the tagged v1.20.0 release earlier this session (and likely earlier releases too, pending the recent Preact migration commits cf1bce4/e5abb62) -- SAM: worth deciding whether a patch release is warranted, this ticket does not decide that.
design: Fixed in commit 85761c4: main.jsx's show() function now detects whether route.view()'s result is a real DOM Node (only the unused comingSoon()/soon:true fallback) or a Preact VNode (every real page today), and calls Preact's own render(vnode, outlet) for the latter instead of the generic mount() helper. mount() itself and its other 4 vanilla-DOM call sites (theme icon swap, app shell mount, chat drawer no-op) are untouched -- this was the minimal-blast-radius fix, not a rewrite of the rendering bridge.
acceptance_criteria: Verified via Playwright against a real running server (not just source inspection): all 11 pre-existing pages plus the new bindings page render real content, zero occurrences of the literal string in any page's main content area. task check passes.
notes: Closed on discovery -- already fixed, tested, and pushed in the same session that found it.
close_reason: Fixed, tested (Playwright against a real isolated server), and pushed as commit 85761c4.

title: Measure and reduce task-agent context amplification
description: PR #635 consumed at least 1,286,449 tokens across baseline repair, analysis, repro, and fix, while the PR footer reported only 997,900. Do not impose a hard token stop: successful and failed tasks are evaluation evidence. Measure prompt/completion/cached usage by stage and iteration, include every agent stage in task totals, enable adaptive history compaction, and bound redundant tool-result replay so task completion remains the authority while efficiency becomes observable and improvable.
acceptance_criteria: Task telemetry attributes prompt, completion, cached, total tokens and iterations by workflow stage; baseline-repair usage is included in task totals; task agents compact redundant accumulated history without imposing a token stop; successful and failed tasks remain comparable; regression coverage and quality gate pass.
notes: Maintainer decision: max_tokens is not desired as a blocker. Optimize context economics and preserve outcomes as metrics.
close_reason: Provider usage is durable by stage, baseline repair is included, model-adaptive compaction is enabled without a token cap, and ai-sdk preserves partial/compaction usage. task check and fresh adversarial review pass.

title: Security: an unauthenticated endpoint must not be able to run an agent
description:
P0 within this epic because the feature's own pitch is the threat model: a public intake surface whose output is an agent with tool access and a repo. Get this wrong and a webhook URL is remote code execution with extra steps.

Non-negotiables to design:

- Per-source authentication. A source registers with a secret (HMAC, as internal/channels/webhook already does per route) before its events can trigger anything. Capture-only for unknown senders is acceptable; triggering is not.
- Human approval before a binding goes live. An operator authoring a binding is a deliberate act; an event arriving is not. Nothing should self-arm.
- Rate and volume limits per source, so capture cannot be used to exhaust disk or drown the inspector.
- Payload content is untrusted input flowing into an agent prompt. Treat prompt injection as expected, not exceptional -- the sender controls that text, and the agent has tools. Bound what a playbook-triggered workflow may do.
- Captured payloads may contain secrets from the sending system. Decide retention, redaction and who can view them; internal/memory/scrubber may already have applicable prior art.

Archie's own principle applies: environmental enforcement over prompt rules. 'The agent should ignore instructions in the payload' is not a control.

title: Security: an unauthenticated endpoint must not be able to run an agent
description:
P0 within this epic because the feature's own pitch is the threat model: a public intake surface whose output is an agent with tool access and a repo. Get this wrong and a webhook URL is remote code execution with extra steps.

Non-negotiables to design:

- Per-source authentication. A source registers with a secret (HMAC, as internal/channels/webhook already does per route) before its events can trigger anything. Capture-only for unknown senders is acceptable; triggering is not.
- Human approval before a binding goes live. An operator authoring a binding is a deliberate act; an event arriving is not. Nothing should self-arm.
- Rate and volume limits per source, so capture cannot be used to exhaust disk or drown the inspector.
- Payload content is untrusted input flowing into an agent prompt. Treat prompt injection as expected, not exceptional -- the sender controls that text, and the agent has tools. Bound what a playbook-triggered workflow may do.
- Captured payloads may contain secrets from the sending system. Decide retention, redaction and who can view them; internal/memory/scrubber may already have applicable prior art.

Archie's own principle applies: environmental enforcement over prompt rules. 'The agent should ignore instructions in the payload' is not a control.
acceptance_criteria: An event from an unauthenticated source can be captured but cannot trigger a workflow; a new binding requires explicit human approval before it arms; per-source rate limits exist; the blast radius of a playbook-triggered workflow is bounded by code rather than by prompt text; retention and visibility of captured payloads is decided and documented.
notes:
2026-08-22: security design decided and documented in docs/prds/webhook-intake-security.md, covering all five non-negotiables from this bead's description:
1. Per-source auth reuses internal/channels/webhook's existing HMAC-SHA256 scheme; capture accepts unsigned events (visible, marked unauthenticated), only authenticated events can ever match a binding.
2. Bindings gain a draft -> pending_approval -> armed state machine; any edit to an armed binding drops it back to pending_approval so approval can't be bypassed by editing. Modeled on telegram's existing dangerousAction/pendingApproval flow (dangerous.go/approval.go).
3. Per-source token-bucket rate limiting (precedent: pairing/store.go's MaxPendingPerPlatform); limit-exceeded is an observable 429, not a silent drop.
4. Blast radius bounded by the SAME code-level controls every task already gets -- gate, diff_cap_lines, sandboxed container, worktree isolation -- no new relaxation for playbook-triggered work, and payload text is ordinary untrusted prompt input, never a trusted instruction.
5. 7-day configurable retention on captured payloads; best-effort redaction reusing gateway/stream.go's sensitiveParameterKey heuristic before persisting; visibility gated by the same dashboard auth as every other webui surface.

This bead's code-level acceptance criteria (capture-can't-trigger, rate limits exist, blast-radius bounded, approval gate) cannot be implemented yet: they constrain t2db.1 (capture), 7d5u.3 (intake family) and t2db.4 (binding), none of which have landed. This document is the contract those beads build against -- do not build any of them without satisfying it. Leaving this bead in_progress rather than closing it; it closes when t2db.1/7d5u.3/t2db.4 land and demonstrably satisfy points 1-5, not before.
close_reason: Closed

title: eda: resolve mid-playbook action failure semantics (execution-time gap 1)
description:
Design-investigation ticket, same shape as the idempotency one above -- produces a design-doc resolution, not implementation. Gates multi-action playbooks (t2db.15 is deliberately single-action to avoid needing this). docs/prds/eda-playbook-engine.md's 'Execution-time gap 1' has no default yet and explicitly says a default must be a stated decision, not something nobody chose.

Grounded by a crew investigation pass (2026-09-03, not committed -- content folded in here): read event-sources-and-reactions.md's producer-only/no-veto/no-mutation language, existing internal/domain/workflow stage-failure conventions (does a failing stage stop/wrap/resume?), and the load-collision report shape (drop+log+report to caller) from t2db.9-.12 as the precedent for how a run outcome should be reported.
design:
Decide and write the resolution into eda-playbook-engine.md:
1. On action N of M failing: stop-on-first-failure (matches this doc's existing anti-clever-recovery bias) vs continue-to-independent-later-actions vs rollback. State which, and why the alternatives were rejected -- don't just restate the doc's existing hedge.
2. What 'rollback' means (likely: nothing, since a posted forge comment isn't revocable) -- state this explicitly rather than leaving it implied.
3. Producer-only interaction: decide whether a playbook reacting to its own action's failure by running compensating actions is in scope -- state the boundary explicitly against event-sources-and-reactions.md's producer-only rule.
4. Condition-failure vs action-failure: J3 (CEL condition eval error -> false, skip, log, continue) is already decided for conditions specifically. State cleanly how this differs from an actual action failure.

STRONG REUSABLE PRECEDENT FOUND IN THIS CODEBASE (verified directly, 2026-09-03) -- read internal/domain/workflow/workflow.go:294-352 (Run/finish/park) before designing anything new. The existing workflow engine already answers a structurally identical question for its own stages, and the answer is precise, not just 'stop on failure':
- A real stage error: stop immediately, set ParkReason (which stage, what error), call park() -- status becomes store.StatusParked, requiring human/retry intervention. This IS this codebase's existing 'stop-on-first-failure, log the outcome, report to caller' pattern -- a playbook run failure should almost certainly reuse the SAME park/report shape (or a directly analogous one) rather than inventing new run-outcome semantics.
- Context cancellation (ctx.Err() != nil, e.g. daemon shutdown mid-stage) is explicitly NOT treated as a failure: the task is left running so existing crash-recovery requeues it; parking here 'would publish a false failure and require manual intervention.' A playbook coordinator dispatching a Module/Workflow action needs the SAME distinction -- a daemon-shutdown interruption mid-action must not be recorded as an action failure, or every restart during a dispatch would falsely mark playbooks as broken.
- A workflow ending without an explicit terminal outcome is itself parked as 'workflow ended without an outcome (definition bug)' -- i.e. an engine-level invariant violation gets its own distinct, honestly-labeled outcome rather than being silently treated as success. Consider whether a playbook run has an analogous 'must end with X' invariant.

This means gap 1 may reduce to: 'reuse park()'s three-way distinction (real failure / shutdown interruption / definition-bug) for playbook runs' rather than a from-scratch design -- read the actual code before deciding whether that reduction actually holds or where a playbook run's shape genuinely differs (e.g. playbooks may not have a Store.Transition-shaped persistence target the way a store.Task does -- confirm what a playbook run's own state, if any, actually gets recorded to).
acceptance_criteria: eda-playbook-engine.md's Execution-time gap 1 section is marked resolved with a stated default (not a list of candidates) and explicit reasoning against event-sources-and-reactions.md's producer-only rule. No code changes required for this ticket to close.
notes: Proposed resolution drafted 2026-09-03 in docs/prds/eda-playbook-engine.md, commit 99eaa7a -- reuses workflow.Run's existing three-way stage-failure distinction. Explicitly marked 'awaiting Sam's sign-off,' not settled.

title: eda: resolve idempotency keying for Module/Channel/Forge actions (execution-time gap 2)
description:
Design-investigation ticket (like the CEL question, archie-core-t2db resolution in eda-playbook-engine.md) -- produces a design-doc resolution, NOT implementation. This is the sharper of the two unresolved execution-time gaps named in docs/prds/eda-playbook-engine.md's 'Execution-time gaps' section: workflow-kind actions inherit idempotency for free via TaskEnvelope; channel/forge/module actions with real side effects have no keying scheme, so a redelivered trigger event (internal/eventbus is at-least-once PublishUnique) would double-fire a comment, a message, or a billed image generation.

Grounded by a crew investigation pass (2026-09-03, further-investigation.md, not committed -- content folded into this ticket): read internal/eventbus's PublishUnique key computation and existing dedup surface, TaskEnvelope's idempotency key minting/consumption path, event-sources-and-reactions.md's decided contract (extend it, don't contradict it), and the CEL context surface in internal/domain/eda/expr (event/actions fields available for key derivation).
design:
Design-decide and write into eda-playbook-engine.md:
1. Granularity: one idempotency key per trigger-event + playbook (whole run dedups) vs per-action key derived from the run key. The doc's stated bias is the former unless a specific action needs finer dedup -- turn that bias into a stated decision.
2. Where the key lives: does a playbook run get its own envelope/context carrying the key, and how does it reach the target position's invocation (Module.Invoke, a future Channel/Forge call)?
3. What 'dedup' does on redelivery: is the whole run skipped, or just the already-fired action? What gets recorded?

STRONG REUSABLE PRECEDENT FOUND IN THIS CODEBASE (verified directly, 2026-09-03) -- do not design a new ledger without reading this first: internal/store/bindings.go already implements exactly this shape for playbook bindings. binding_dispatches table, unique on (binding_id, capture_id), written via RecordDispatch's 'INSERT OR IGNORE' -- a duplicate insert returns the sentinel ErrAlreadyDispatched, which dispatchBindings (internal/daemon/daemon.go:479) treats as a normal 'another cycle raced us' outcome, not an error. This is a proven, tested, at-most-once dispatch guarantee across cycles AND daemon restarts, for the exact same kind of problem (don't re-fire a binding for a capture it already dispatched). The playbook-run idempotency key almost certainly should reuse this exact pattern: a new ledger table (or a generalization of binding_dispatches) keyed on (playbook_id, event_id) or (playbook_id, trigger_event_identity), written with the same INSERT OR IGNORE + sentinel-error convention. Read internal/store/bindings.go:29-61,351-378 and internal/daemon/daemon.go:479-514 before designing anything -- this may reduce gap 2 to 'apply the existing pattern to a new key shape' rather than new design.
4. Key derivation: a CEL-reachable expression over event fields, or a stable hash of event-identity+playbook-id -- pick one and justify it against the expr package's actual context surface, and against how capture identity is derived today (check what 'capture_id' actually is -- likely a stable hash or row id from the same capture pipeline a playbook trigger would also read).
acceptance_criteria: eda-playbook-engine.md's Execution-time gap 2 section is marked resolved with a stated decision (not a survey of options) covering granularity, key storage/lookup, redelivery behavior, and key derivation. Consistent with event-sources-and-reactions.md's existing idempotency contract -- explicitly states how it extends rather than contradicts it. No code changes required for this ticket to close.
notes: Proposed resolution drafted 2026-09-03 in docs/prds/eda-playbook-engine.md, commit 99eaa7a -- reuses internal/store/bindings.go's binding_dispatches ledger shape. Explicitly marked 'awaiting Sam's sign-off,' not settled. Surfaced two concrete prerequisites while drafting: t2db.15's Playbook struct needs an ID/Version (doesn't have one), and DispatchInput needs a task identity threaded through (doesn't have one either) -- both stated honestly as blockers for implementation, not glossed over.

title: fix stale wfextract go:generate directive; audit pluginextract/secretextract drift
description:
Discovered 2026-09-03 while scoping archie-core-t2db.13 (Module position). Two separate, pre-existing issues, unrelated to the playbook engine work -- do not fix as a drive-by inside that ticket.

1. internal/domain/workflow/wfextract/wfextract.go's //go:generate directive still targets 'github.com/samcharles93/archie-core/internal/workflow', a path that has not existed since the domain migration (7e896c9, 2026-08-07 - the package moved to internal/domain/workflow). The committed generated file was hand-patched at some point to import the new path, but the directive itself was never fixed. Net effect: 'go generate ./...' has been broken repo-wide (at least for wfextract) since that migration, silently, for anyone who hasn't tried running it.

2. Running 'go generate ./...' anyway (to see what breaks) also produced real, substantive diffs in internal/plugin/pluginextract and internal/secret/secretextract's generated symbol tables -- new wrapper types (Host, Module) appearing that are NOT in the currently-committed, in-production symbol tables. This means the Yaegi plugin and secret-engine extension surfaces have been running against stale, incomplete generated symbol tables for an unknown period: interpreted plugin/secret-engine code may be unable to reference types it should have access to. This is a latent correctness gap with real blast radius on two extension surfaces, not cosmetic drift.
design:
Two-part fix, do not conflate:
1. Fix wfextract's directive to point at internal/domain/workflow (matching what the generated file already imports). Verify 'go generate ./internal/domain/workflow/wfextract/...' now succeeds and produces output identical (or intentionally different, documented why) to what's committed.
2. For pluginextract/secretextract: do NOT blindly regenerate-and-commit. First determine why they're stale (when did plugin.go/secret's Engine gain the types the fresh generation adds -- git log on internal/plugin/plugin.go and internal/secret's engine files vs. when the generated files were last touched) and whether any existing test exercises a Yaegi plugin/secret-engine referencing the missing types (if none does, that's itself a coverage gap worth noting). Regenerate, gofumpt, and add/confirm a test that would have caught the drift, before committing the regenerated symbol tables -- this is a correctness-sensitive change to two live extension surfaces and needs real verification, not a mechanical re-run.
acceptance_criteria: 'go generate ./...' completes without error across the whole repo. wfextract's directive matches its actual package path. pluginextract/secretextract regeneration (if done) is backed by a test demonstrating the previously-missing types are now reachable from interpreted code, and task check passes. No behavior change to existing plugins/secret engines that were already working (regression-tested, not assumed).
close_reason: Fixed and gate-verified as e3a20f6 (pushed to main). wfextract directive now targets internal/domain/workflow; 'go generate ./...' completes repo-wide. All four extract surfaces regenerated; nil-guards re-applied on interface wrappers (documented IMPORTANT note restated in wfextract package doc). Previously-missing symbols proven reachable from interpreted code: wfextract (Forger/Reviewer/Trees/routing loaders) and pluginextract (Host/Module/Manifest/NewHost/HostAPIVersion) via new reachability tests; secretextract exports were current (nil-guard drift only). Red-then-green verified: fresh regen wipes guards -> guard tests panic -> re-apply -> pass. task check clean (113/113 UI, exit 0).

title: StageCommitPush discards baseline-fix commits when build makes no changes
description:
Confirmed via carina production logs (task 6, chat-spawned synthetic test task, 2026-09-02). StageBaselineGate (internal/domain/workflow/implement.go:37) found the repo's gate red at the base commit, spent 405,004 tokens/14 iterations genuinely fixing two broken pre-existing tests, and committed the fix locally via tc.Trees.CommitAll (implement.go:104) -- verified passing. plan and build stages then correctly found nothing else to do for the (synthetic, content-free) task. StageCommitPush -> closeNoChangesIssue (steps.go:56) decides 'no changes' purely from tc.BuildNoChanges, which the build AgentStage sets from its own len(res.Changes)==0 (implement.go:176) -- it has zero awareness that StageBaselineGate already committed real changes two stages earlier. Never pushed, never opened a PR; the entire worktree containing a real, gate-verified fix for genuinely broken tests was discarded when the task closed as 'merged: completed -- no changes required'.

Cost: 669,421 tokens burned to fix a real bug that then evaporated. This recurs: any task that hits the same red baseline pays the identical tax again since the fix never lands. Evidence a prior incident already happened: an orphaned 'fix: baseline gate repair' commit (e49f3cd) sits on a stale, unmerged branch (fix/441-archied-repos-entries-cant-span-more-than-one-forge) from an earlier occurrence.
design: Fix direction: either (a) StageBaselineGate sets a flag /flips tc.BuildNoChanges appropriately when it commits, or (b) StageCommitPush's no-changes branch checks the worktree's actual diff against the base branch (tc.Trees, similar to StageDiffCap's ChangedLines) instead of trusting tc.BuildNoChanges alone. Prefer (a): cheaper, and keeps the diff-against-base check (which already exists for StageDiffCap) from being computed twice per task.
acceptance_criteria: A task whose baseline-fix stage committed real changes, but whose plan/build stages found nothing further to do, still pushes and opens a PR carrying the baseline-fix commit -- it must never be silently discarded. tc.BuildNoChanges (or StageCommitPush's decision) accounts for what StageBaselineGate already committed, not just the build stage's own diff. Regression test reproduces the exact scenario (baseline-fix commits, build stage reports zero changes) and proves a PR opens. task check passes.
close_reason: Fixed via a new TaskContext.BaselineFixed flag: StageBaselineGate sets it when its own CommitAll reports a real committed change (implement.go:104-111). The build stage's OnResult only sets BuildNoChanges when its own diff is empty AND BaselineFixed is false (implement.go:177), so a baseline-only fix can no longer be masked as 'no changes'. StageCommitPush itself now calls CommitAll directly and pushes whenever either a new commit was made OR BaselineFixed is true (steps.go), instead of erroring on 'nothing to commit' when the real change already sits on the branch from the baseline-fix commit. Two new regression tests (TestStageCommitPushPushesBaselineFixEvenWithNothingNewToCommit, TestStageBaselineGateSetsBaselineFixedWhenItCommits) plus a guard test that the old empty-tree error still fires without a baseline fix. task check clean.

title: task_logs truncates at 50KB with no pagination, so full logs are unreachable
description:
The task_logs chat tool caps its response at 50 KB and offers no way to fetch the rest. An operator asking the agent to retrieve or archive a task's logs gets a silently clipped window, and the agent has no mechanism to page past it. Observed 2026-08-24: asked to save a full transcript and agent logs, the agent could only produce a partial archive and had to document the truncation as a limitation rather than satisfy the request.

The failure compounds with archie-core-p1bl (errors logging as `{}`): a truncated log of uninformative errors leaves an operator with nothing at all, precisely when a task is stuck.

## What is needed

Truncation itself is legitimate -- a tool result must be bounded, and unbounded log text would blow the model's context. The defect is that truncation is TERMINAL: there is no continuation, no offset/cursor, no way to narrow the window, and the caller cannot tell how much was lost.

Establish first where the cap is applied (the task_logs tool in internal/gateway/task_tools.go and whatever log reader it calls in internal/logging -- note internal/logging owns the on-disk format end to end and internal/webui parses nothing, per CLAUDE.md, so the reader is the right place for range support).

Design points to decide:
- A cursor or offset so successive calls walk the whole log, rather than always returning the same head or tail.
- Filters that make bounded retrieval useful rather than merely possible: by level (errors only), by time range, by stage.
- The response must state explicitly that it was truncated and how much remains, so the agent can report honestly instead of implying completeness.
- Consider whether bulk retrieval belongs in a tool result at all, or whether the right answer for "save the full logs" is to write the file and deliver it via the new send_file path (archie-core-absb), keeping the tool result small.

## Acceptance Criteria

An operator can obtain a task's complete logs through the agent, by paging or by file delivery; a truncated response says so and reports what remains rather than ending silently; level and time-range filtering exist so a bounded call can still answer a specific question; the cap remains enforced so no single response can exhaust the model's context; tests cover a log larger than the cap and assert that repeated calls retrieve all of it without gaps or duplication.
close_reason: task_logs cursor pagination, level/time filters, and honest truncation reporting

title: Task logs serialise errors to an empty object, destroying diagnostics
description:
Error values in task logs sometimes render as an empty JSON object, so the one field that says WHY something failed carries no information. Observed in production task logs 2026-08-24, in the same stream:

  {"time":"...","level":"ERROR","message":"handle failed","fields":{"err":{}}}
  {"time":"...","level":"ERROR","message":"handle failed","fields":{"err":"stage re…"}}

Same message, same field, two different encodings -- one useful, one useless. The empty-object form is what an operator hits when diagnosing a stuck task, which is exactly when the log is the only evidence available.

## Likely mechanism (to be confirmed, not assumed)

`{}` is what encoding/json produces for a struct with no exported fields. A custom error type (a struct implementing `error` via a value or pointer receiver, with all fields unexported) marshals to `{}` rather than to its Error() string, because encoding/json does not consult the error interface. Errors that happen to be `*errors.errorString` or `fmt.Errorf` results go through a different path and survive as text.

Start at internal/logging (attrs.go and its tests already reference a "handle failed" record, so the attribute handling is there) and establish where an `error` attribute is converted for the JSONL sink. The fix is to render errors through their Error() string -- and, where the error carries structured context worth keeping, to do so ADDITIONALLY rather than instead.

## Why P1

Sam's words: "LOGGING! ... this is another critical requirement." Diagnosis of every other defect depends on it. Two separate investigations this week were slowed by log output that recorded that something failed without recording what.

Note this compounds archie-core-1ysw-era debugging and the parked-task investigation: an operator seeing `{"err":{}}` has strictly less information than one seeing no log line at all, because the empty object implies the error was captured.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Arrange for a code path that logs a custom error type (unexported fields) as an `err` attribute.
2. Read the task's JSONL log via the dashboard, /api logs, or the task_logs tool.
3. Observe `"err":{}` where the message should be.
4. Compare with a path that logs a fmt.Errorf value and observe `"err":"..."` in the same file.

## Acceptance Criteria

Every error logged as an attribute renders its Error() text in the JSONL sink regardless of the concrete error type; a custom error type with only unexported fields is covered by a test asserting the message survives; structured context on an error is preserved in addition to, never instead of, the message; a regression test fails against the current encoder; no log line can report an error as an empty object.
close_reason: Shipped in 6a23f8d: logging resolves every non-nil error attribute through Error(), with custom unexported-field and typed-nil regression coverage; included in archied v1.18.0.

title: Dashboard mutations 403 behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy: Origin check ignores X-Forwarded-Proto
description:
Every operator action from the dashboard -- Stop, Cancel, Retry, Approve, Reject, Abandon, Archive -- fails with HTTP 403 in the production deployment. Observed 2026-08-24: `POST https://archie.catlow.cloud/api/tasks/3/action` returned 403 in 7ms with a 30-byte body. This left the operator with no way to stop a running task from the web UI at all.

## Root cause

`authorizeTaskMutation` (internal/webui/api_tasks.go:197-221) derives the expected Origin scheme from the daemon's OWN connection:

    wantScheme := "http"
    if r.TLS != nil {
        wantScheme = "https"
    }
    ...
    if ... || !strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, wantScheme) || !strings.EqualFold(u.Host, r.Host) {
        http.Error(w, "cross-origin mutation refused", http.StatusForbidden)

archied runs behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS (confirmed: archie.catlow.cloud redirects to auth.catlow.cloud for forward auth, and the request was HTTP/2 to the proxy). The daemon therefore receives a PLAIN HTTP connection, so `r.TLS == nil` and `wantScheme == "http"`, while the browser correctly sends `Origin: https://archie.catlow.cloud`. Scheme mismatch -> 403 on every mutation.

`X-Forwarded-Proto` is never consulted anywhere in the codebase (`grep -rn 'X-Forwarded' internal/webui/ internal/config/` returns nothing).

## Evidence the body confirms which branch fired

There are exactly two 403 paths in this handler. Their response bodies differ in length:
- "missing CSRF header\n" = 20 bytes
- "cross-origin mutation refused\n" = 30 bytes

The observed response was 30 B, so the Origin comparison is what rejected it, NOT the CSRF header. The dashboard is sending X-Archie-CSRF correctly.

## Why this is P1

It is a total loss of the operator control surface in the supported deployment shape. It also removes the documented remedy for other faults: archie-core-0dic leaves a stopped task's row reading `running`, and `Parked`'s retry action is the stated recovery for a review that fails closed (docs/prds/adversarial-self-review.md section 4) -- both assume dashboard actions work.

Note the deployment model is explicitly plural (CLAUDE.md "Deployment model": several supported shapes, systemd is not required), so "runs behind a proxy" is a first-class configuration, not an edge case.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Serve archied behind any TLS-terminating reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy, Traefik, or a forward-auth proxy such as Authelia), with the daemon listening on plain HTTP.
2. Load the dashboard over https and press Stop on a running task.
3. Observe `POST /api/tasks/<id>/action` -> 403, body "cross-origin mutation refused".
4. The same build works when reached directly over http, or over https terminated by the daemon itself, which is why this does not reproduce in local development.

## Acceptance Criteria

Dashboard mutations succeed when archied is behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy; the effective scheme is derived from X-Forwarded-Proto (and the effective host from X-Forwarded-Host where applicable) ONLY when the request arrives from a trusted proxy, configured explicitly -- an unconditional trust of these headers would let any client forge the Origin check and defeat the CSRF protection this function exists to provide; direct (non-proxied) deployments keep their current strict behaviour; tests cover proxied-https, direct-http, direct-https, and a spoofed X-Forwarded-Proto from an untrusted source; the config surface and its default are documented in config.example.toml and the deployment profiles.
notes:
CONFIRMED LIVE against production 2026-08-25 via Playwright, signed in as the operator.

Reproduced the dashboard's own Stop request from the loaded page:

  fetch('/api/tasks/3/action', {method:'POST',
    headers:{'X-Archie-CSRF':'1','Content-Type':'application/json'},
    body:'{"action":"stop"}'})

Result: status 403, body exactly "cross-origin mutation refused\n" (30 bytes), with location.origin = https://archie.catlow.cloud and location.protocol = https:.

This settles which of the two 403 branches fires. The request carried a correct X-Archie-CSRF header and same-origin credentials, so it passed the CSRF check and was rejected by the Origin comparison in authorizeTaskMutation. Combined with the deployment shape (archie.catlow.cloud 302s to auth.catlow.cloud for forward auth, so TLS terminates at the proxy and the daemon sees plain HTTP), the scheme comparison is the failing term: browser Origin scheme 'https' vs the daemon's computed wantScheme 'http' from r.TLS == nil.

The dashboard confirms the operator impact at the same time: the header reads '1 running' and task #3 is still listed as running (that stale row is archie-core-0dic, a separate defect). So in production the operator currently cannot stop task #3 from either surface -- the web UI is 403'd by this bug, and chat /stop leaves the row reading running via 0dic.

Related UX gap worth its own bead rather than folding in here: the only user-visible signal was a console error, 'Failed to load resource: the server responded with a status of 403'. The dashboard surfaced nothing actionable in the UI itself, which is why this went unnoticed until devtools were opened.
DEPLOYMENT CONFIRMED from /work/infra/automation (Ansible):

roles/traefik/templates/archie.yml.j2 defines router 'archie-webui' on the 'websecure' entrypoint with 'tls: certresolver', i.e. Traefik terminates TLS. roles/traefik/defaults/main.yml:17-18 give:
  traefik_archie_webui_domain: archie.catlow.cloud
  traefik_archie_webui_backend_url: http://10.36.25.188:8484   <-- PLAIN HTTP

So archied receives a plain-HTTP request and computes wantScheme='http', while the browser sends Origin: https://archie.catlow.cloud. That is the whole bug.

Two details that make the fix precise and low-risk:

1. Only the SCHEME term fails. Traefik forwards the original Host by default (passHostHeader), so u.Host == r.Host already matches. The Origin check does not need host rewriting for this deployment -- honouring the forwarded scheme is sufficient. Keep X-Forwarded-Host support optional/secondary rather than assuming it is needed.

2. The header archied needs is ALREADY ARRIVING. Traefik sets X-Forwarded-Proto: https on proxied requests by default. Nothing in the infrastructure has to change; archied simply never reads it. That also means the fix is verifiable against this exact deployment without an infra edit.

Auth context, for whoever implements: the same router injects 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' via the archie-webui-token middleware, behind authelia@docker forward auth. So the trusted-proxy boundary is well defined here -- requests reaching :8484 have already passed Traefik. Whatever trust configuration is added must still DEFAULT to not trusting X-Forwarded-* , because an operator running archied directly exposed would otherwise let any client forge Origin and defeat the CSRF protection entirely.
close_reason: Shipped in 16f9456: explicitly configured trusted forwarded headers drive effective Origin validation, with direct/proxied/spoofed regression coverage; included in archied v1.18.0.

title: Stopped tasks stay 'running' forever: terminal writes ride the cancelled context
description:
/stop reports success and genuinely does stop the container, but the task row is never updated, so the dashboard, /status and task_list all show the task as running indefinitely. Observed 2026-08-24: task #3 was stopped and was still displayed as running the following day.

## Root cause

`Daemon.runViaAgent` (internal/daemon/daemon.go:1010-1100) writes its terminal state with the SAME context that was just cancelled, and discards the result:

    reply, err := d.requestTaskRun(ctx, task.ID, data)   // returns ctx.Err() on /stop
    if err != nil {
        _ = d.Store.Transition(ctx, task.ID, store.StatusRunning, store.StatusParked, "taskrun request failed: "+err.Error())

`store.Transition` writes through `tx.ExecContext(ctx, ...)` (internal/store/store.go:358-365), so on a cancelled context the write fails immediately and the `_ =` throws the error away. The row stays `running` with nothing left to correct it.

There are SIX such writes in runViaAgent (grant unavailable, grant failed, encode failed, request failed, decode failed, run failed). Every one is unreachable in exactly the situation it exists for -- cancellation -- because cancellation is what invalidates the context it writes with.

`cleanupTerminalTaskWorktree` (daemon.go:897) has the same defect: it re-reads via `d.Store.TaskByID(ctx, ...)` and returns early on error, so a cancelled task also skips worktree cleanup.

## Why the container is NOT the problem

`Pool.Release` already gets this right and is the precedent for the fix: it detaches deliberately with `context.WithTimeout(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), 10*time.Second)` and documents why -- "the most important reason a task is on its way out is that it was cancelled... Teardown is cleanup, so it gets its own deadline rather than inheriting the caller's cancellation." So teardown works; only state recording is broken.

## Contributing factor

`StoreTaskController.StopRunning` (internal/gateway/tasks.go:227) deliberately writes no terminal state, documented as "A stopped task unwinds through its own error paths and lands wherever that leaves it, usually parked". That assumption is now false: the unwind path cannot record anything, so nothing lands. Note `CancelChatTask` (the /cancel path) DOES write state explicitly and is unaffected.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start an autonomous task so it reaches `running` with a live archie-agent container.
2. Issue `/stop` from chat (or Stop from the dashboard).
3. Observe the container is stopped and removed by Pool.Release.
4. Observe the task row is still `status = running` in the store, in `task_list`, in `/status` and on the dashboard.
5. Wait: nothing ever corrects it. Only a daemon restart re-queues it, via the crash-recovery path that re-queues tasks left `running`.

## Acceptance Criteria

Terminal state writes on the cancellation path use a context that survives cancellation (`context.WithoutCancel`, with its own timeout, mirroring Pool.Release); their errors are logged rather than discarded; a stopped task reaches a terminal state observable in the store, task_list and the dashboard without a daemon restart; cleanupTerminalTaskWorktree also runs for a cancelled task; a regression test cancels a task mid-run and asserts the row is no longer `running`, and fails against the current code.
notes:
Timeline correction: the task was observed still 'running' roughly ONE HOUR after /stop, not a day (an earlier note said a day; that was inferred wrongly from a date rollover). An hour is if anything stronger evidence, since no plausible refresh interval covers it.

Chronology correction: the agent's pre-/stop task_list reading 'still marked running' is NOT evidence of this bug -- nothing had stopped the task at that point, so it was reporting correctly. The genuine evidence is (a) the row still 'running' an hour after /stop, and (b) the code path itself, which predicts exactly that and was found by reading runViaAgent rather than from the transcript.

Scope note: this bug explains a stale ROW only. It does not explain a still-live container, because container.Pool.Release deliberately detaches from the cancelled context and does tear down. If a container is ever found alive after /stop, that is a SEPARATE defect, not this one.

title: [EPIC] Adversarial self-review before archie opens a PR
description:
Archie enforces gates on every PR it opens, but it does not run the adversarial review CLAUDE.md makes mandatory for every change in this repo: a fresh reviewer that did not write the code, told to assume every line is wrong, working a defined checklist, where a surviving finding blocks the work. It is the one discipline the project requires of its contributors and exempts itself from.

Why it matters, with evidence rather than assertion: on 2026-08-20/21 the update-verification change (PR #530) passed task check at every checkpoint -- exit 0, golangci-lint 0 issues, gofumpt clean -- and three adversarial passes still found six real defects, two of them blocking. A 'dev' version placeholder would have reported healthy updates as failures, and an 'unknown' install claim was still being worded as confirmed success. The gates were green throughout and would have stayed green. This is CLAUDE.md's own recorded lesson: tests catch behaviour that breaks, not behaviour that quietly starts meaning something else.

Archie is unusually well placed to do this. It already runs each task in an isolated container and worktree, so it can spawn a reviewer that genuinely never saw the implementation -- not a second opinion from the same context pretending to be fresh, which is the failure mode of every single-context tool. The isolation boundary built for safety is what makes honest self-review possible.

What the operator gets: a PR that arrives with a findings section -- what was checked, what was found, what was fixed, what survived. A surviving finding parks the task as waiting_human instead of opening a PR that looks ready and is not. Review shifts from hunting for bugs to adjudicating findings.

The risk that kills the feature is a reviewer that cries wolf. Findings must be adversarially confirmed before they surface, and the reviewer must be able to report zero findings on properties it checked and cleared. Calibration is the feature, not the finding count.
close_reason: Duplicate epic; canonical versions are archie-core-t2db (#541), archie-core-7d5u (#547), and archie-core-h019 (#552) with proper work breakdown

title: Findings contract: a structured review result the workflow can act on
description:
The reviewer's output must be data the workflow can branch on, not prose a human has to read to find out whether the PR is safe to open. Prose is what makes a review advisory; structure is what lets a finding block.

Define the finding type in the workflow domain (the domain declares the contract it needs; it never names who implements it). At minimum a finding carries: file and line, a one-sentence defect, a concrete failure scenario (inputs/state -> wrong output), a verdict distinguishing CONFIRMED from PLAUSIBLE, and a disposition once acted on (fixed / skipped / no_change_needed).

The CONFIRMED/PLAUSIBLE split is load-bearing and must not be collapsed into a single boolean: only confirmed findings may block, or the feature degrades into crying wolf and the operator learns to skim past it.
close_reason: Duplicate; work tracked under canonical epic

title: Design: adversarial self-review stage (one-page decision in docs/prds/)
description:
No settled design exists for this in docs/architecture/, so under the scope-discipline rule merged as PR #533 the design comes first -- briefly and decisively -- and is not finished until a diff follows it.

Decide and record, in one page under docs/prds/: where the reviewer runs (reuse the per-task container pool, or a separate short-lived container); what it is given (diff plus originating issue, and explicitly what it must NOT be given); the findings contract and who owns the type; what a surviving finding does to the task lifecycle; and how the reviewer's model/effort is configured.

Constraints from the repo that the design must respect: dependency direction is cmd -> app -> {domain, infrastructure}, so the reviewer contract belongs to the workflow domain and the execution to infrastructure/app. Agent execution is a data boundary. The model never runs git. Prefer environmental enforcement over prompt rules -- 'the reviewer cannot see the implementation' must be a property of how it is launched, not an instruction in its prompt.

Do not write an architecture document, migration plan or review campaign. One page that decides.
close_reason: Duplicate; work tracked under canonical epic

title: Wire review as an implement-workflow stage: after gates, before PR open
description:
Sequence matters. The review runs after gates pass -- there is no point reviewing code that does not build or test -- and before the PR is opened, because the point is to not spend the operator's attention on a PR that is not ready.

A surviving CONFIRMED finding must not open a PR. It parks the task as waiting_human with the findings attached, which is the existing lifecycle state for 'a human needs to look at this' and needs no new state. Per CLAUDE.md, a finding that survives blocks closing the work; it does not get waved through.

Scope to the implement workflow first. Routing to tdd/bootstrap/feasibility is a later decision -- feasibility in particular produces a document rather than a diff, so 'review the diff' may not even apply.
close_reason: Duplicate; work tracked under canonical epic

title: Reviewer runs in a context that provably never saw the implementation
description:
This is the whole feature. A reviewer that shares the implementer's context is a second opinion from the same mind, and it will rationalise the same mistakes -- which is exactly the failure mode CLAUDE.md's 'never self-certified by the implementer' rule exists to prevent.

Archie already has the machinery: each task runs in an isolated container against its own worktree. Launch the reviewer the same way, seeded only with the diff and the originating issue. It must not receive the implementer's conversation, its notes, its reasoning, or its own claims about what it did.

Per 'environmental enforcement over prompt rules', isolation must be a property of construction, not a sentence in the prompt. The agent cannot talk its way out of a context it was never given. Assert it in a test rather than assuming it: a test that would fail if implementer context were threaded through.
close_reason: Duplicate; work tracked under canonical epic

title: [EPIC] Event sources and typed reactions: archie as an extensible platform
description:
Goal: let archie react to things happening -- forge activity, inbound callers, schedules -- and let extensions hook those reactions, without a generic untyped event bus.

Two findings shape this, both verified in the tree on 2026-08-21.

1. ARCHIE HAS TWO EVENT NEEDS AND ONE BUS. internal/events is documented as 'archied's in-process observability stream' with 'bounded per-subscriber buffers that DROP on overflow, so a stalled dashboard connection can never apply backpressure to the task engine'. Publish is fire-and-forget; subscribers get a read-only channel and cannot influence anything. Correct for the dashboard, wrong for reactions: a hook that silently misses events under load and cannot affect an outcome is worse than no hook, because it looks like it ran. Reactions need at-least-once delivery and the ability to change what happens. Do not bolt reactions onto events.Bus.

2. THE OBVIOUS DESIGN IS PROHIBITED, DELIBERATELY. The tau model this is drawn from dispatches generically: DispatchEvent(ctx, eventName string, sessionID, ...) to out-of-process gRPC plugins. archie's approved foundation (docs/architecture/plugins-and-extensions.md) forbids that shape -- the generic plugin contract stays metadata-only and MUST NOT expose untyped hooks. plugin.Plugin is Name()/Version() only, enforced by internal/plugin/architecture_test.go and by the plugin engine rule in ARCHITECTURE.md. tau already carries the scar the rule avoids: TestUnload_DoesNotWaitForInFlightDispatch exists because a stuck plugin blocked plugin unload.

The reconciliation, and why this is an epic rather than a feature: separate INBOUND (callers push work in -- forge webhook, chat webhook, cron, channel) from REACTION (extensions respond to something that happened). Inbound becomes a typed source/intake capability family with an owning registry. Reactions become typed capability families owned by the domain whose semantics they affect. 'Webhooks aligned to types of callers' is exactly the typed-family model applied to intake: the instinct is right, the generic bus is what has to go.

Near-term payoff: archie reacts to an issue being labelled the moment it happens, instead of up to poll_interval later.
close_reason: Duplicate epic; canonical versions are archie-core-t2db (#541), archie-core-7d5u (#547), and archie-core-h019 (#552) with proper work breakdown

title: Shared webhook mechanics: HMAC verification, per-source rate limiting, payload redaction
description:
NARROWED 2026-08-22 from this bead's prior scope, which bundled capture-storage and an approval state machine into a single 'shared mechanics' package. On reflection those are not genuinely shared yet:

- Capture STORAGE is t2db.1's job -- it depends on the NATS-vs-SQLite decision 7d5u.2 owns, and building a storage engine here would either duplicate or contradict that. This package may be USED by t2db.1's capture path, but does not own persistence.
- The draft/pending_approval/armed state machine belongs to the entity that has that state -- t2db.4's binding -- not a generic package. There is exactly one consumer (bindings) today; per 'extract into a shared primitive on the second real consumer, never in anticipation of one,' building it here now would be speculative.

What remains, and is genuinely storage-agnostic and reusable by any inbound HTTP source regardless of what consumes it:

1. HMAC-SHA256 verification -- generalize internal/channels/webhook/webhook.go's existing unexported validateHMAC into an exported function here, and have that package call into it instead of keeping its own copy. One implementation of signature checking, not two that can drift.
2. Per-source rate limiting -- a token bucket keyed by source ID (not global), so one noisy sender cannot exhaust another's budget. Limit-exceeded is an observable rejection, not a silent drop, per t2db.5's decision.
3. Payload redaction -- generalize internal/gateway/stream.go's unexported sensitiveParameterKey/redactToolParameters heuristic (matches token/secret/password/passwd/api_key/apikey/authorization/credential/cookie/private_key against normalized JSON keys) into a reusable, storage-agnostic transform any capture path can apply before persisting.
close_reason: Duplicate; work tracked under canonical epic

title: Reaction delivery via embedded NATS, no external server required
description:
Reactions need at-least-once delivery distinct from the lossy events.Bus (see epic description). The delivery mechanism is NATS -- that part is settled, not a design question. What's open is deployment shape.

VERIFIED 2026-08-22: config.NATSConfig.URL empty currently means 'no NATS, use SQLite ClaimNext' (internal/config/config.go:573-582). That fallback was designed for task distribution working without a broker at all. It was never meant to generalise to 'archie has no NATS' as a permanent architectural stance -- the intended second deployment shape alongside an external NATS server was always NATS EMBEDDED (in-process), not a different eventbus.

github.com/nats-io/nats-server/v2 is already a direct dependency and is proven to work in this codebase: internal/infrastructure/agenttransport/nats/transport_test.go and others already start a real embedded server via nats-server/v2/test for tests. It has just never been wired into production startup -- cmd/archied only knows 'external URL configured' vs 'fall back to SQLite'. No new library, no new bus, no architectural gap to design around: this is 'wire the dependency we already have and already test against into the daemon's own startup path.'

Design questions that remain, now correctly scoped: does an embedded NATS instance replace the SQLite fallback outright for single-process deployments, or run alongside it; what config controls embedded vs external vs disabled; does the daemon own the embedded server's lifecycle the same way it owns everything else (start/stop paired with daemon start/stop, per the shutdown-ordering rules in ARCHITECTURE.md).
close_reason: Duplicate; work tracked under canonical epic

title: Design: event sources, reaction delivery, and how extensions hook them
description:
No settled design covers this. docs/architecture/plugins-and-extensions.md settles the PLUGIN FRAMEWORK (metadata-only contract, typed capability families, owning registries) but says nothing about event sources, reaction delivery, or intake. Under the scope-discipline rule merged as PR #533, that means design first -- one page, decisive -- then a diff.

Decide and record in docs/prds/:

1. THE HEADLINE QUESTION, which changes everything downstream: do extensions react in-process through typed capability families (what the approved rule mandates), or out-of-process like tau's generic DispatchEvent? If out-of-process generic dispatch is genuinely wanted, docs/architecture/plugins-and-extensions.md is an APPROVED document and must be amended first -- CLAUDE.md's organisation rule is explicit that you change the doc before the rule it states. Do not quietly work around it.

2. Reaction delivery. events.Bus drops on overflow by design and must stay that way for the dashboard. Decide whether reactions get a second in-process bus with at-least-once delivery, or ride the existing NATS eventbus (internal/infrastructure/eventbus), which already has durable semantics and the work-queue traps documented in CLAUDE.md.

3. Whether a reaction may INFLUENCE an outcome (veto, mutate, add work) or only observe. This is the difference between a hook and a subscriber, and it determines whether ordering and failure semantics matter. If a reaction can block, decide what a slow or crashed extension does -- tau's answer was a dispatch timeout, and it still deadlocked unload once.

4. The typed source/intake family: its interface, its owning registry, and how a source declares what it produces.

Respect dependency direction: cmd -> app -> {domain, infrastructure}. A domain declares the contract; app wires implementations. Cross-cutting packages may be imported by any layer and import none.
close_reason: Duplicate; work tracked under canonical epic

title: Idempotency and poll/webhook parity: never double-dispatch, never lose work
description:
Webhooks deliver at-least-once, out of order, and sometimes not at all. Polling is the opposite: slow but eventually consistent. Running both (intake='both') is the honest production configuration, and it is also where the two failure modes meet.

Two things must hold. A single issue event must not start two tasks because the webhook and the next poll both saw it. And a webhook outage must not silently stop work -- if the receiver is wedged or the ingress is down, polling has to pick the work up, which is the entire argument for keeping it.

Note archie-core-...-286 (WebhookAdapter: idempotency cache) already exists for the chat adapter. Decide whether that mechanism generalises to intake or whether forge dispatch needs its own key; do not build a second one by accident.

The silent-failure shape to design against is the one this codebase keeps hitting: a path that looks like it is working because nothing errors. A webhook receiver that has silently stopped delivering looks identical to a repo with no activity.
close_reason: Duplicate; work tracked under canonical epic

title: GitHub forge webhook receiver behind a feature flag
description:
The concrete autonomy win: react to an issue being assigned or labelled the moment it happens, instead of up to poll_interval (default 60s) later.

Verified absent on 2026-08-21: internal/forge/ and internal/daemon/ contain zero webhook references, and no bead tracked forge-event intake before this epic. internal/channels/webhook exists but is a CHAT channel -- it routes inbound text through gateway.Router for LLM processing, a peer of Telegram and email. It is not forge intake and should not be bent into it.

Ship as a source in the typed intake family, off by default: [forge] intake = 'poll' (default) | 'webhook' | 'both'. Verify GitHub's HMAC signature. Reuse the label/assignee dispatch predicate the poller already uses -- do NOT reimplement it, since it just took a fix (3209a1f, refusing to poll on an empty label match) and two implementations will drift.

Deployment reality from CLAUDE.md: archied may run on a host, in a container, or behind no public ingress at all. A webhook receiver that assumes a reachable public URL will not fit every profile, which is exactly why polling has to remain a first-class option rather than a legacy fallback.
close_reason: Duplicate; work tracked under canonical epic

title: [EPIC] Event capture and no-code playbooks: turn any inbound webhook into an agentic workflow
description:
The pitch, in the operator's words: point any app's outgoing webhook at archie, open archie, SEE the event that just arrived with its real payload, map the fields you care about, bind them to an agentic workflow, save. No code change, no redeploy, no restart. Adding a new integration stops being a development task.

Why this is different from n8n or Power Automate rather than a copy of them: their terminal node is a deterministic connector. Archie's is an AGENT with a repo, a worktree, tools and a gate. 'When Sentry reports a new issue in this project, open a PR that fixes it' is one binding here and an entire product elsewhere.

The design insight that makes it buildable: you cannot write a payload mapper against a payload you have not seen. Schema-by-example requires real recent events to map against, which means archie must CAPTURE events it does not yet understand -- including ones with no binding at all -- and retain them long enough to design against. That is also the strongest argument for putting inbound events on NATS JetStream rather than the lossy in-process bus: durable, replayable, retention-bounded, and already deployed. The capture requirement and the transport choice are the same decision.

Sequence: capture unrecognised events -> inspect real payloads in the UI -> map fields by example -> bind matcher+mapping to a workflow -> the next matching event runs it.

This is a public, unauthenticated-by-default intake surface whose output is an agent with tool access. Security is not a later hardening pass; it is a first-class child of this epic.
close_reason: Duplicate epic; canonical versions are archie-core-t2db (#541), archie-core-7d5u (#547), and archie-core-h019 (#552) with proper work breakdown

title: Map payload fields by example, from a real captured event
description:
Pick a captured event, click through its payload, and bind JSON paths to named fields the workflow will receive. Schema by example, not schema by specification.

The hard part is not the happy path, it is drift. A mapping authored against one payload will eventually meet a payload where the path is missing, null, or a different type -- the sending app shipped a change nobody told you about. That must fail LOUDLY and land somewhere the operator sees, not silently pass an empty string into an agent prompt. An agent handed a blank field will confabulate around it, which turns a schema change into an agent doing confident nonsense in a repo.

Support a preview: given this mapping and this captured event, show exactly what the workflow would receive. Never ship a mapping the operator has not seen resolve against real data.

title: Event inspector: see real inbound payloads in the dashboard
description:
The operator-facing half of capture. A live view of recent inbound events: source, arrival time, and the actual payload, pretty-printed and explorable.

This is the screen that makes the feature feel like magic: you hit 'send test webhook' in the other app, alt-tab to archie, and the event is sitting there. Latency from arrival to visible matters more than it looks -- it is the difference between a design loop and a guessing game.

Show unbound events prominently. An event nothing is listening to is not noise here, it is the queue of integrations waiting to be built.
close_reason: Duplicate; work tracked under canonical epic

title: Capture inbound events archie does not yet understand
description:
The precondition for everything else. Today an unrecognised inbound request is rejected; for schema-by-example it must be RECORDED, because you cannot map a payload you have never seen.

Accept, store and retain inbound events with no binding: raw body, headers, source, arrival time, and the identity that sent it. Retention must be bounded -- an open capture endpoint is an unbounded disk write, and this is exactly the kind of surface an attacker fills.

Strong argument for NATS JetStream as the store rather than the in-process events.Bus: durable, replayable, retention-bounded natively, already deployed. Note the constraint though -- internal/infrastructure/eventbus/nats/doc.go states 'when no NATS URL is configured the daemon uses its local SQLite claim flow instead; nothing here is required for single-process operation'. NATS is currently OPTIONAL. Decide deliberately whether capture requires it (making this feature unavailable in single-process deployments) or degrades to SQLite, and record which -- do not let it become a hard dependency by accident.
close_reason: Duplicate; work tracked under canonical epic

title: Playbook binding: matcher + mapping + workflow, editable at runtime
description:
The object that ties it together. A binding is: a matcher (which inbound events does this apply to), a mapping (which fields the workflow receives), and a target agentic workflow.

Runtime-editable is the whole point -- creating or changing a binding must not require a redeploy or a daemon restart. That has real consequences the design must face:

- Bindings are persisted state, not config. They live in the store, not config.toml, because operators create them from the UI while the daemon runs.
- They need versioning. A binding that starts a task should record WHICH version ran, or a later edit makes historical task provenance a lie.
- Matcher ambiguity needs a defined resolution: two bindings matching one event either both run, or the more specific wins, or it is an error. Pick one and say so.
- A binding referencing a workflow that no longer exists must fail visibly at bind time, not at 3am when the event arrives.

title: Clean abandoned untracked files on retry
description: Prepare refresh hard-resets tracked files but retains untracked files; CommitAll later stages and publishes them during the next attempt.
acceptance_criteria: A regression test proves an untracked file left by an interrupted attempt is absent after retry and cannot appear in ChangedFiles or the next commit; deliberate .git control files remain intact.

Remaining defect fixed in 037ee7c: SkipDir on a .git gitdir *file* aborted the whole walk, so cleaning silently no-opped for linked/adopted worktrees. Regression test TestCleanUntrackedHandlesGitdirFile.

title: Make worktree directory keys collision-free
description: Manager.Dir flattens owner and repo with a hyphen, so distinct repositories such as a-b/c and a/b-c share a task directory for equal issue numbers.
acceptance_criteria: Distinct owner/repo tuples always map to distinct contained paths; sequential and concurrent collision regressions cannot reuse, delete, reset, or push the other repository's clone.
