description:
The pitch, in the operator's words: point any app's outgoing webhook at archie, open archie, SEE the event that just arrived with its real payload, map the fields you care about, bind them to an agentic workflow, save. No code change, no redeploy, no restart. Adding a new integration stops being a development task.

Why this is different from n8n or Power Automate rather than a copy of them: their terminal node is a deterministic connector. Archie's is an AGENT with a repo, a worktree, tools and a gate. 'When Sentry reports a new issue in this project, open a PR that fixes it' is one binding here and an entire product elsewhere.

The design insight that makes it buildable: you cannot write a payload mapper against a payload you have not seen. Schema-by-example requires real recent events to map against, which means archie must CAPTURE events it does not yet understand -- including ones with no binding at all -- and retain them long enough to design against. That is also the strongest argument for putting inbound events on NATS JetStream rather than the lossy in-process bus: durable, replayable, retention-bounded, and already deployed. The capture requirement and the transport choice are the same decision.

Sequence: capture unrecognised events -> inspect real payloads in the UI -> map fields by example -> bind matcher+mapping to a workflow -> the next matching event runs it.

This is a public, unauthenticated-by-default intake surface whose output is an agent with tool access. Security is not a later hardening pass; it is a first-class child of this epic.
acceptance_criteria: An operator can point a new external webhook at archie, see its payload in the UI without writing code, map fields, bind it to a workflow, and have the next matching event run that workflow -- with no redeploy and no daemon restart. A binding cannot go live without explicit human approval.

title: GitHub forge webhook receiver behind a feature flag
description:
The concrete autonomy win: react to an issue being assigned or labelled the moment it happens, instead of up to poll_interval (default 60s) later.

Verified absent on 2026-08-21: internal/forge/ and internal/daemon/ contain zero webhook references, and no bead tracked forge-event intake before this epic. internal/channels/webhook exists but is a CHAT channel -- it routes inbound text through gateway.Router for LLM processing, a peer of Telegram and email. It is not forge intake and should not be bent into it.

Ship as a source in the typed intake family, off by default: [forge] intake = 'poll' (default) | 'webhook' | 'both'. Verify GitHub's HMAC signature. Reuse the label/assignee dispatch predicate the poller already uses -- do NOT reimplement it, since it just took a fix (3209a1f, refusing to poll on an empty label match) and two implementations will drift.

Deployment reality from CLAUDE.md: archied may run on a host, in a container, or behind no public ingress at all. A webhook receiver that assumes a reachable public URL will not fit every profile, which is exactly why polling has to remain a first-class option rather than a legacy fallback.
acceptance_criteria: With intake='webhook', a labelled issue starts a task without waiting for the poll interval; an invalid HMAC is rejected and logged; intake='poll' behaves exactly as today; the dispatch predicate is shared with the poller, not duplicated; the flag defaults to poll.
close_reason: GitHub webhook receiver shipped: [forge] intake=poll|webhook|both, shared MatchesDispatch predicate (case-insensitive assignee, case-sensitive label) consumed by poller and receiver, HMAC-verified, publishes via shared PublishTask. Adversarial self-review found and fixed 3 real defects (boot-crashing secret-resolve hard-fail under intake=both, assignee case-sensitivity mismatch vs GitHub's own filter, silent multi-identity misdispatch) before landing. task check + lint clean. Committed 41e43dc.

title: Idempotency and poll/webhook parity: never double-dispatch, never lose work
description:
Webhooks deliver at-least-once, out of order, and sometimes not at all. Polling is the opposite: slow but eventually consistent. Running both (intake='both') is the honest production configuration, and it is also where the two failure modes meet.

Two things must hold. A single issue event must not start two tasks because the webhook and the next poll both saw it. And a webhook outage must not silently stop work -- if the receiver is wedged or the ingress is down, polling has to pick the work up, which is the entire argument for keeping it.

Note archie-core-...-286 (WebhookAdapter: idempotency cache) already exists for the chat adapter. Decide whether that mechanism generalises to intake or whether forge dispatch needs its own key; do not build a second one by accident.

The silent-failure shape to design against is the one this codebase keeps hitting: a path that looks like it is working because nothing errors. A webhook receiver that has silently stopped delivering looks identical to a repo with no activity.
acceptance_criteria: A duplicate delivery of the same forge event starts exactly one task; with intake='both', disabling the webhook path still results in the work being picked up by polling; a wedged or non-delivering webhook receiver is observable rather than indistinguishable from an idle repo.
close_reason: Investigated first: the dedup mechanism (TaskEnvelope.IdempotencyKey + PublishUnique + JetStream Nats-Msg-Id dedup) and the shared dispatch predicate were already fully wired by 7d5u.4 -- no double-dispatch code change was needed. Closed the two real gaps: (1) internal/infrastructure/eventbus/nats/dedup_test.go is a new regression test proving PublishUnique actually suppresses a duplicate publish on the same WorkQueuePolicy stream ARCHIE_TASKS uses in production; (2) internal/forge/webhook/receiver.go gained Status()/GET support tracking authenticated deliveries vs successful publishes separately, so a wedged or non-delivering receiver is observable rather than indistinguishable from an idle repo. AC's poll/webhook parity clause (disabling webhook still polls) is satisfied architecturally with no code change possible to violate it -- verified Cycle()/Run() never reference cfg.Forge.Intake anywhere in internal/daemon; only setupForgeWebhook in cmd/archied/bootstrap.go gates the webhook HTTP server. Adversarial review pass (fresh subagent, -race) found zero blocking issues; closed two minor coverage gaps it flagged. [Closure restored 2026-08-24: originally closed 2026-08-22, lost when the beads DB was rebuilt (.beads.backup-pre-recovery).]

title: Design: event sources, reaction delivery, and how extensions hook them
description:
No settled design covers this. docs/architecture/plugins-and-extensions.md settles the PLUGIN FRAMEWORK (metadata-only contract, typed capability families, owning registries) but says nothing about event sources, reaction delivery, or intake. Under the scope-discipline rule merged as PR #533, that means design first -- one page, decisive -- then a diff.

Decide and record in docs/prds/:

1. THE HEADLINE QUESTION, which changes everything downstream: do extensions react in-process through typed capability families (what the approved rule mandates), or out-of-process like tau's generic DispatchEvent? If out-of-process generic dispatch is genuinely wanted, docs/architecture/plugins-and-extensions.md is an APPROVED document and must be amended first -- CLAUDE.md's organisation rule is explicit that you change the doc before the rule it states. Do not quietly work around it.

2. Reaction delivery. events.Bus drops on overflow by design and must stay that way for the dashboard. Decide whether reactions get a second in-process bus with at-least-once delivery, or ride the existing NATS eventbus (internal/infrastructure/eventbus), which already has durable semantics and the work-queue traps documented in CLAUDE.md.

3. Whether a reaction may INFLUENCE an outcome (veto, mutate, add work) or only observe. This is the difference between a hook and a subscriber, and it determines whether ordering and failure semantics matter. If a reaction can block, decide what a slow or crashed extension does -- tau's answer was a dispatch timeout, and it still deadlocked unload once.

4. The typed source/intake family: its interface, its owning registry, and how a source declares what it produces.

Respect dependency direction: cmd -> app -> {domain, infrastructure}. A domain declares the contract; app wires implementations. Cross-cutting packages may be imported by any layer and import none.
acceptance_criteria: A one-page decision in docs/prds/ answering all four questions, naming the packages it will touch, and stating explicitly whether plugins-and-extensions.md needs amending. It decides rather than surveys.
notes: CORRECTION 2026-08-22 (second): decision question 2 in this bead's description asked whether reactions get a second in-process bus or ride the existing NATS eventbus. That framing is wrong -- there is no 'or'. NATS is the settled transport; the only open axis is external-server vs embedded, not NATS vs something else. Do not design a second bus. See archie-core-7d5u and archie-core-7d5u.2 for the corrected framing and the verified state of github.com/nats-io/nats-server/v2 as an already-present, test-proven, production-unwired dependency.
close_reason:
Decided and documented in docs/prds/event-sources-and-reactions.md, satisfying this bead's own acceptance criterion (a one-page decision naming the packages it touches and stating whether plugins-and-extensions.md needs amending -- it does not).

Answers: (1) in-process typed families, no out-of-process dispatch -- archie has no existing extension-process boundary and neither epic's stated payoff needs one. (2) Reaction delivery reuses internal/eventbus's Publisher/Consumer contract (PublishUnique + Ack/Nak already provide at-least-once with dedup), but NOT the existing nats.Client as-is: it hardcodes Retention: jetstream.WorkQueuePolicy (client.go:65) for the competing-consumer ARCHIE_TASKS stream, which silently starves a second consumer on overlapping subjects per CLAUDE.md's documented trap -- reactions need fan-out, so retention needs to become a Config field and reactions get their own stream. (3) Reactions in these two epics are producer-only (cheap wake via curator's WakeOnPrimaryInput pattern, or produce real work via the existing pollNATS->publishTask path) -- no veto/mutate-in-flight-work capability is being built here; that belongs to archie-core-h019 if it's ever needed. (4) No single generic Source interface -- forge intake reuses workintake.TaskEnvelope unchanged (its IdempotencyKey is already keyed on owner/repo/number, not delivery source, so a webhook-sourced envelope naturally dedups against a poll-discovered one for free); chat webhook stays internal/channels/webhook, unmodified; what's genuinely new and shared is a small cross-cutting package for HMAC/rate-limit/approval/capture mechanics, owned by neither domain.

title: Reaction delivery via embedded NATS, no external server required
description:
Reactions need at-least-once delivery distinct from the lossy events.Bus (see epic description). The delivery mechanism is NATS -- that part is settled, not a design question. What's open is deployment shape.

VERIFIED 2026-08-22: config.NATSConfig.URL empty currently means 'no NATS, use SQLite ClaimNext' (internal/config/config.go:573-582). That fallback was designed for task distribution working without a broker at all. It was never meant to generalise to 'archie has no NATS' as a permanent architectural stance -- the intended second deployment shape alongside an external NATS server was always NATS EMBEDDED (in-process), not a different eventbus.

github.com/nats-io/nats-server/v2 is already a direct dependency and is proven to work in this codebase: internal/infrastructure/agenttransport/nats/transport_test.go and others already start a real embedded server via nats-server/v2/test for tests. It has just never been wired into production startup -- cmd/archied only knows 'external URL configured' vs 'fall back to SQLite'. No new library, no new bus, no architectural gap to design around: this is 'wire the dependency we already have and already test against into the daemon's own startup path.'

Design questions that remain, now correctly scoped: does an embedded NATS instance replace the SQLite fallback outright for single-process deployments, or run alongside it; what config controls embedded vs external vs disabled; does the daemon own the embedded server's lifecycle the same way it owns everything else (start/stop paired with daemon start/stop, per the shutdown-ordering rules in ARCHITECTURE.md).
acceptance_criteria: A single-process deployment with no external NATS URL configured still gets reaction delivery via an embedded NATS instance; the daemon starts and stops the embedded server as part of its own lifecycle; no second eventbus type is introduced; internal/infrastructure/eventbus/nats is reused as the transport rather than duplicated.
notes: 2026-08-22, from docs/prds/event-sources-and-reactions.md: do not reuse the existing nats.Client's stream creation as-is. internal/infrastructure/eventbus/nats/client.go:65 hardcodes Retention: jetstream.WorkQueuePolicy -- correct for ARCHIE_TASKS (task distribution, one consumer claims each message) and wrong for reactions, which need fan-out (every registered reaction sees every matching event). Two reactions on overlapping subjects under WorkQueuePolicy hit the exact trap CLAUDE.md documents: the second consumer silently gets nothing. Config.StreamName/Config.Subjects are already composition-supplied (config.go:30-38); Retention is not parameterized and needs to become a Config field, defaulting to today's WorkQueuePolicy so ARCHIE_TASKS is unaffected, with reactions getting a second stream under a fan-out-capable policy and their own subject namespace.
close_reason: Embedded NATS wired into production startup: mode=embedded/external/off resolves from url, daemon owns the in-process server lifecycle, Retention parameterized for a future fan-out reaction stream. task check + lint clean; adversarial review zero surviving findings. Committed 2c7db34.

title: Shared webhook mechanics: HMAC verification, per-source rate limiting, payload redaction
description:
NARROWED 2026-08-22 from this bead's prior scope, which bundled capture-storage and an approval state machine into a single 'shared mechanics' package. On reflection those are not genuinely shared yet:

- Capture STORAGE is t2db.1's job -- it depends on the NATS-vs-SQLite decision 7d5u.2 owns, and building a storage engine here would either duplicate or contradict that. This package may be USED by t2db.1's capture path, but does not own persistence.
- The draft/pending_approval/armed state machine belongs to the entity that has that state -- t2db.4's binding -- not a generic package. There is exactly one consumer (bindings) today; per 'extract into a shared primitive on the second real consumer, never in anticipation of one,' building it here now would be speculative.

What remains, and is genuinely storage-agnostic and reusable by any inbound HTTP source regardless of what consumes it:

1. HMAC-SHA256 verification -- generalize internal/channels/webhook/webhook.go's existing unexported validateHMAC into an exported function here, and have that package call into it instead of keeping its own copy. One implementation of signature checking, not two that can drift.
2. Per-source rate limiting -- a token bucket keyed by source ID (not global), so one noisy sender cannot exhaust another's budget. Limit-exceeded is an observable rejection, not a silent drop, per t2db.5's decision.
3. Payload redaction -- generalize internal/gateway/stream.go's unexported sensitiveParameterKey/redactToolParameters heuristic (matches token/secret/password/passwd/api_key/apikey/authorization/credential/cookie/private_key against normalized JSON keys) into a reusable, storage-agnostic transform any capture path can apply before persisting.
acceptance_criteria: webhookguard.VerifyHMAC replaces internal/channels/webhook's private copy with no behaviour change (its existing tests still pass); a per-source rate limiter rejects over-budget requests observably; a redaction function matches the same key heuristic already proven in gateway/stream.go; the package has zero imports of any domain, infrastructure or app package.
notes: --notes=2026-08-22: merged to main as f3d3d32 (PR #534, squash of aa23ac9+46401ab+ce4f945).
close_reason:
Built internal/webhookguard: VerifyHMAC (behavior-preserving extraction from internal/channels/webhook, which now calls it instead of keeping a private copy), RateLimiter (per-source token bucket, independent budgets, observable rejection), RedactPayload (key-name heuristic matching gateway/stream.go's marker list, but -- deliberately unlike that function -- redacts only values under sensitive keys and leaves ordinary strings/numbers/bools untouched, since a captured payload exists to be inspected for field mapping in t2db.3).

All four acceptance criteria met and independently confirmed by a fresh adversarial review with zero surviving findings: HMAC extraction is byte-for-byte behavior-preserving (diffed against the deleted function); rate limiter hand-traced correct on two scenarios plus race-clean under -race; redaction's divergence from gateway/stream.go verified by reading both functions side by side; zero non-stdlib imports confirmed by grep. The reviewer also mutation-tested both the redaction and rate-limit guards (disabled each in turn) and confirmed the test suite catches both, then reverted and re-verified go test -race and git status were clean.

task check exit 0, golangci-lint 0 issues (one forcetypeassert finding was caught and fixed properly during build, not suppressed), gofumpt clean. All 10 pre-existing internal/channels/webhook tests pass unmodified; the one now-redundant unit test was removed with a comment pointing to where its coverage relocated.

title: [EPIC] Event sources and typed reactions: archie as an extensible platform
description:
Goal: let archie react to things happening -- forge activity, inbound callers, schedules -- and let extensions hook those reactions, without a generic untyped event bus.

Two findings shape this, both verified in the tree on 2026-08-21.

1. ARCHIE HAS TWO EVENT NEEDS AND ONE BUS. internal/events is documented as 'archied's in-process observability stream' with 'bounded per-subscriber buffers that DROP on overflow, so a stalled dashboard connection can never apply backpressure to the task engine'. Publish is fire-and-forget; subscribers get a read-only channel and cannot influence anything. Correct for the dashboard, wrong for reactions: a hook that silently misses events under load and cannot affect an outcome is worse than no hook, because it looks like it ran. Reactions need at-least-once delivery and the ability to change what happens. Do not bolt reactions onto events.Bus.

2. THE OBVIOUS DESIGN IS PROHIBITED, DELIBERATELY. The tau model this is drawn from dispatches generically: DispatchEvent(ctx, eventName string, sessionID, ...) to out-of-process gRPC plugins. archie's approved foundation (docs/architecture/plugins-and-extensions.md) forbids that shape -- the generic plugin contract stays metadata-only and MUST NOT expose untyped hooks. plugin.Plugin is Name()/Version() only, enforced by internal/plugin/architecture_test.go and by the plugin engine rule in ARCHITECTURE.md. tau already carries the scar the rule avoids: TestUnload_DoesNotWaitForInFlightDispatch exists because a stuck plugin blocked plugin unload.

The reconciliation, and why this is an epic rather than a feature: separate INBOUND (callers push work in -- forge webhook, chat webhook, cron, channel) from REACTION (extensions respond to something that happened). Inbound becomes a typed source/intake capability family with an owning registry. Reactions become typed capability families owned by the domain whose semantics they affect. 'Webhooks aligned to types of callers' is exactly the typed-family model applied to intake: the instinct is right, the generic bus is what has to go.

Near-term payoff: archie reacts to an issue being labelled the moment it happens, instead of up to poll_interval later.
acceptance_criteria: A forge webhook triggers work behind a feature flag with polling still available as a backstop; inbound callers register through one typed family rather than bespoke wiring per caller; reactions have delivery guarantees distinct from the lossy observability bus; the generic plugin contract remains metadata-only and internal/plugin/architecture_test.go still passes.
notes:
CORRECTION 2026-08-22 (second): the earlier summary I gave characterized 'NATS is currently optional' as an open architectural gap for this epic to navigate around. That's wrong, and Sam corrected it directly: NATS was never meant to be optional as a technology. What's optional is running a standalone NATS SERVER -- config.NATSConfig.URL empty falls back to the existing SQLite ClaimNext flow (internal/config/config.go:573-582, internal/infrastructure/eventbus/nats/doc.go:24). The intended second deployment shape is NATS EMBEDDED (in-process, no external server to stand up), not 'no NATS, use some other eventbus'. There is no other eventbus in scope, was never meant to be one, and this epic must not introduce one.

Current code state, verified: github.com/nats-io/nats-server/v2 (the embeddable NATS server package) is already a direct, non-indirect dependency, and is genuinely used to spin up an in-process server -- but only inside _test.go files (internal/infrastructure/agenttransport/nats/transport_test.go and others use github.com/nats-io/nats-server/v2/test to run tests against a real embedded server). It has never been wired into production as an actual deployment mode. So embedded NATS is proven to work in this codebase's own test harness, and the gap is purely that production startup only knows 'external URL configured' vs 'no NATS, fall back to SQLite' -- there is no production code path that starts nats-server in-process.

This changes 7d5u.2 (reaction delivery) materially: 'ride the existing NATS eventbus, or a second in-process bus' was the wrong framing. The actual question is whether reaction delivery requires an external NATS deployment or can run on an embedded NATS instance so single-process deployments still get it -- not whether to use NATS at all versus some other bus. If embedded NATS is wired for reaction delivery, capture (t2db.1) gets it too essentially for free, since they were flagged as needing the same underlying decision.

title: Reviewer runs in a context that provably never saw the implementation
description:
A reviewer that shares the implementer's context is a second opinion from the same mind, and it will rationalise the same mistakes -- the failure mode CLAUDE.md's "never self-certified by the implementer" rule exists to prevent.

UNBLOCKED 2026-08-25. The mechanism is decided in docs/prds/adversarial-self-review.md section 1 (rewritten, superseding the version q15y invalidated): the reviewer is an `agent.Subagent` run from inside the task-scoped archie-agent worker. ai-sdk v0.1.22 is already the pinned version, so no SDK bump. This adds no host executor, no second Pool.Acquire and no nested container lifecycle -- the open question the supersession left.

Two isolations are required and only one is free:

- CONVERSATION isolation is structural. `Subagent.Run` (agent/subagent.go:76-96) calls GenerateText with Prompt set and Messages never populated, so the implementer's history has no code path into the nested run. This is the property to assert in the required test.
- WORKSPACE isolation is ours to build. A sub-agent shares the parent's process, working directory and credentials, so the `.git`-free snapshot survives from the original design and is load-bearing: `git archive <commit> | tar -x` into a fresh scratch directory BESIDE the task worktree, plus `diff.patch` and `issue.md`. Stripping `.git` is what makes commit messages, branch name and reflog structurally unreachable rather than merely undisclosed.

Three construction rules:
1. `Subagent.Tools` gets a distinct read-only toolset rooted at the snapshot. NEVER the worker's own toolset -- it carries the worktreerpc publication grant, so a reviewer holding it could push the branch it exists to block.
2. Call `Run()`, not `Tool()`. `Tool()` would let the implementer's own model elect to review itself, which is the self-certification this feature prevents. It also avoids Tool()'s two-step-parent and recursion footguns.
3. Findings return via a closure-captured capture tool, not the return value -- `Run` yields only text. Because the sub-agent is in-process, the capture tool's Go func appends to a []workflow.ReviewFinding the stage owns. Read that slice EVEN WHEN `Run` returns an error: findings already captured survive, so a reviewer that logged three defects then hit its step limit still yields those three.

## Acceptance Criteria

The reviewer is launched with only the snapshot, diff.patch and issue.md; a test fails if implementer context reaches it, asserting isolation as a construction fact rather than prompt text; the reviewer's prompt instructs it to assume every line is wrong until proven correct; the mechanism reuses agent.Subagent inside the existing worker rather than inventing a second execution path; the reviewer's toolset is read-only, rooted at the snapshot, and provably excludes the worktreerpc publication grant; captured findings are recovered even when Run returns an error.
acceptance_criteria: The reviewer is launched with only diff + issue; a test fails if implementer context reaches it; the reviewer's prompt instructs it to assume every line is wrong until proven correct; the mechanism reuses the existing container/worktree isolation rather than inventing a second one.
notes: BLOCKED 2026-08-24: not implementable as specified. docs/prds/adversarial-self-review.md is marked 'Superseded; requires redesign before implementation' -- superseded by the full-task worker boundary landed in archie-core-q15y. Its mechanism for this bead was a daemon-side second container.Pool.Acquire plus an in-process agentexec path; q15y.2 and q15y.3 removed BOTH call sites, so the isolation mechanism this bead reuses no longer exists. Needs a design decision first: how a fresh reviewer receives a .git-stripped snapshot from INSIDE the existing task-scoped archie-agent worker, without introducing a host executor or a nested container lifecycle. Do not implement against the superseded PRD. The sibling bead h019.2 (findings contract) is unaffected and is being implemented, since it is a pure domain type with no execution dependency.
close_reason: Implemented as agent.Subagent inside the task-scoped archie-agent worker (internal/app/agentworker/review.go). Conversation isolation is structural (Subagent.Run only sends a prompt, never message history -- verified against a fake chat.Provider). Workspace isolation via new worktree.Manager.Snapshot (.git-free export of HEAD's tracked files into a scratch dir beside the task worktree). Reviewer's toolset is read-only (read/grep/find) rooted at the snapshot, never the worker's own toolset -- verified as a construction fact that the toolset contains no write/edit/shell tool and cannot read outside the snapshot dir. Findings captured via a typed record_finding tool appending to a slice the stage owns, surviving a Subagent.Run error when findings were already captured.

title: Wire review as an implement-workflow stage: after gates, before PR open
description:
Sequence matters. The review runs after gates pass -- there is no point reviewing code that does not build or test -- and before the PR is opened, because the point is to not spend the operator's attention on a PR that is not ready. The slot is between StageDiffCap() and StageOpenPR() in internal/domain/workflow/implement.go.

A surviving CONFIRMED finding must not open a PR. Per CLAUDE.md, a finding that survives blocks closing the work; it does not get waved through.

LIFECYCLE CORRECTION (2026-08-25): this bead previously said "parks the task as waiting_human", which names two different states in the actual machine (internal/taskstate/taskstate.go:44-59). docs/prds/adversarial-self-review.md section 4 decided this: use store.StatusParked, following StageDiffCap's existing precedent (steps.go:91-94) -- a stage-computed policy stop with a Detail explaining why, before PR open. Parked's available actions, retry and abandon, are the right shape: fix the flagged code and retry, or abandon/override a false positive. WaitingHuman's approve/reject actions have no referent here because there is no PR yet to approve or reject.

Blocking is workflow.ReviewBlocking (shipped in h019.2): Verdict == confirmed AND Level == error. A PLAUSIBLE finding never blocks, however severe its level claims to be.

FAIL-CLOSED (decided 2026-08-25): a review that fails to RUN is distinct from a review that ran and found nothing, and it must not open a PR. A sub-agent that errors, is truncated, or produces no conclusion yields ReviewStatusNotRun, for which Passed() is false and Blocking() is also false -- the contract deliberately refuses to guess, and this stage resolves it as park. Rationale: Repo.ReviewEnabled is opt-in, so an operator who turned the gate on wants the gate, and a provider outage silently degrading into "PR opened unreviewed" is what they were buying protection against. Accepted cost: a transient model error parks a task, and Parked's retry action is the remedy. The park Detail must say the review did not run, never that it passed.

Scope to the implement workflow first. Routing to tdd/bootstrap/feasibility is a later decision -- feasibility in particular produces a document rather than a diff, so "review the diff" may not even apply.

Also adds to internal/config: Models["reviewer"] (falling back to Models["builder"], no schema change) and Repo.ReviewEnabled bool (default false).

## Acceptance Criteria

An implement task with a clean gate and no confirmed findings opens a PR as it does today; one with a surviving confirmed finding parks as store.StatusParked with findings recorded in Detail and opens no PR; a review that fails to run also parks, with a Detail that says so rather than implying a pass; a warn-level or plausible finding does not block; the stage is observable in the task's running(workflow:stage) status and emits task events despite the nested run being non-streaming; retry after operator action re-runs the stage; the stage is inert unless Repo.ReviewEnabled is true.
acceptance_criteria: An implement task with a clean gate and no confirmed findings opens a PR as it does today; one with a surviving confirmed finding parks as waiting_human with findings recorded and opens no PR; the stage is observable in the task's running(workflow:stage) status; retry after operator action re-runs the review.
close_reason: StageReview wired into the implement workflow between StageDiffCap and StageOpenPR. Fail-closed: not-run or a confirmed error-level finding parks (store.StatusParked) with findings in Detail; warn/plausible findings never block. Inert unless Repo.ReviewEnabled (new config field, default false); Models["reviewer"] falls back to Models["builder"]. task check clean, golangci-lint clean. Committed 8db8a17.

title: Design: adversarial self-review stage (one-page decision in docs/prds/)
description:
No settled design exists for this in docs/architecture/, so under the scope-discipline rule merged as PR #533 the design comes first -- briefly and decisively -- and is not finished until a diff follows it.

Decide and record, in one page under docs/prds/: where the reviewer runs (reuse the per-task container pool, or a separate short-lived container); what it is given (diff plus originating issue, and explicitly what it must NOT be given); the findings contract and who owns the type; what a surviving finding does to the task lifecycle; and how the reviewer's model/effort is configured.

Constraints from the repo that the design must respect: dependency direction is cmd -> app -> {domain, infrastructure}, so the reviewer contract belongs to the workflow domain and the execution to infrastructure/app. Agent execution is a data boundary. The model never runs git. Prefer environmental enforcement over prompt rules -- 'the reviewer cannot see the implementation' must be a property of how it is launched, not an instruction in its prompt.

Do not write an architecture document, migration plan or review campaign. One page that decides.
acceptance_criteria: A one-page decision exists under docs/prds/ answering: reviewer isolation mechanism, inputs and forbidden inputs, findings contract owner, lifecycle effect of a surviving finding, and model/effort configuration. It decides rather than surveys, and cites the packages it will touch.
close_reason: One-page decision written at docs/prds/adversarial-self-review.md: reviewer runs in a second workspace (container or in-process) pointed at a .git-stripped snapshot of the reviewed commit, never the implementer's worktree; findings contract is workflow.ReviewFinding, owned by internal/domain/workflow, reported via a structured capture tool; a surviving error-level finding sets StatusParked (not WaitingHuman -- epic wording named two different states, this resolves which); model/effort reuse the existing Models[role] map and per-stage budget override, gated by a new opt-in Repo.ReviewEnabled so h019.4 doesn't gate every repo on an uncalibrated reviewer before h019.5 lands. [Closure restored 2026-08-24: originally closed 2026-08-22, lost when the beads DB was rebuilt (.beads.backup-pre-recovery).]

title: Findings contract: a structured review result the workflow can act on
description:
The reviewer's output must be data the workflow can branch on, not prose a human has to read to find out whether the PR is safe to open. Prose is what makes a review advisory; structure is what lets a finding block.

Define the finding type in the workflow domain (the domain declares the contract it needs; it never names who implements it). At minimum a finding carries: file and line, a one-sentence defect, a concrete failure scenario (inputs/state -> wrong output), a verdict distinguishing CONFIRMED from PLAUSIBLE, and a disposition once acted on (fixed / skipped / no_change_needed).

The CONFIRMED/PLAUSIBLE split is load-bearing and must not be collapsed into a single boolean: only confirmed findings may block, or the feature degrades into crying wolf and the operator learns to skim past it.
acceptance_criteria: A finding type exists in internal/domain/workflow with file, line, summary, failure scenario, verdict and disposition; it is serialisable across the agent-execution data boundary; a review result with zero findings is representable and distinct from a review that did not run.
close_reason: Implemented: workflow.ReviewFinding + ReviewReport in internal/domain/workflow/review_findings.go, merged 53bb841. The domain owns the type; gate.Finding was used as a shape precedent only, not reused, so the review contract is not coupled to the Yaegi gate's evolution. Blocking requires Verdict==confirmed AND Level==error, so a PLAUSIBLE finding never blocks however severe it claims to be. ReviewStatus makes 'ran and found nothing' structurally distinct from 'never ran' -- Passed() is false for a zero-value report, and the distinction does not rest on nil-vs-empty-slice. JSON round-trip covered; Line 0 is preserved (no omitempty) for whole-file findings. Review found and fixed a duplicate package doc comment and a redundant ReviewBlocking/BlockingReviewFindings alias pair. task check green. Fresh adversarial review clean across 8 dimensions; I independently mutation-tested the blocking rule: dropping the verdict check fails 5 tests (incl. plausible_error_MUST_NOT_block) and dropping the level check fails 5 more, so the tests genuinely pin both halves.

title: [EPIC] Adversarial self-review before archie opens a PR
description:
Archie enforces gates on every PR it opens, but it does not run the adversarial review CLAUDE.md makes mandatory for every change in this repo: a fresh reviewer that did not write the code, told to assume every line is wrong, working a defined checklist, where a surviving finding blocks the work. It is the one discipline the project requires of its contributors and exempts itself from.

Why it matters, with evidence rather than assertion: on 2026-08-20/21 the update-verification change (PR #530) passed task check at every checkpoint -- exit 0, golangci-lint 0 issues, gofumpt clean -- and three adversarial passes still found six real defects, two of them blocking. A 'dev' version placeholder would have reported healthy updates as failures, and an 'unknown' install claim was still being worded as confirmed success. The gates were green throughout and would have stayed green. This is CLAUDE.md's own recorded lesson: tests catch behaviour that breaks, not behaviour that quietly starts meaning something else.

Archie is unusually well placed to do this. It already runs each task in an isolated container and worktree, so it can spawn a reviewer that genuinely never saw the implementation -- not a second opinion from the same context pretending to be fresh, which is the failure mode of every single-context tool. The isolation boundary built for safety is what makes honest self-review possible.

What the operator gets: a PR that arrives with a findings section -- what was checked, what was found, what was fixed, what survived. A surviving finding parks the task as waiting_human instead of opening a PR that looks ready and is not. Review shifts from hunting for bugs to adjudicating findings.

The risk that kills the feature is a reviewer that cries wolf. Findings must be adversarially confirmed before they surface, and the reviewer must be able to report zero findings on properties it checked and cleared. Calibration is the feature, not the finding count.
acceptance_criteria: An implement-workflow task runs an adversarial review after gates pass and before the PR is opened; the reviewer provably cannot see the implementer's context; a surviving confirmed finding blocks PR creation and parks the task; findings and their disposition are visible on the PR and the dashboard.

title: Chat/task agent persona is overconfident: presents unverified claims as verified, fabricates infrastructure details
description:
The chat assistant (archie, running via the Telegram/webui gateway) repeatedly
presents unverified or fabricated information with false confidence, and only
retracts it when directly challenged. This is a persona/system-prompt problem,
not a model quality problem -- reproduced on more than one underlying model.

Two concrete instances from a live Telegram transcript (2026-08-15):

1. Fabricated infrastructure: asked "are logs going anywhere else?", the
   assistant invented an entire second log-shipping subsystem ("Hermes
   gateway") with specific fake file paths
   (/home/sam/.hermes/profiles/local-agent/logs/) that do not exist anywhere
   in archie-core, and stated it as verified fact ("I confirmed the web UI
   token and task lifecycle messages are there"). When challenged ("Is there
   something in the codebase which tells you you're Hermes?"), it admitted
   the paths were invented and carried forward from unrelated, unverified
   context.

2. Overclaimed verification: asked "Why did that last task fail?", the
   assistant answered with a bulleted list explicitly labelled "Verified
   details" (attempt count, iteration count, token count, exact model name).
   When pressed with "You checked it?", it admitted the model name and
   change count were "overstated" -- i.e. it labelled unverified specifics as
   verified the first time, and only corrected itself under direct
   challenge.

The common shape: confident, specific claims presented as fact/verified
first; a walked-back, hedged correction only appears after the user
explicitly challenges it. This erodes trust in every claim the assistant
makes about system state, since the default posture is confident assertion
rather than "I have/haven't actually checked this."
notes: Root cause is believed to be the persona/system-prompt layer (internal/gateway/ BuildSystemPrompt + persona templates), not model selection -- reproduced across models per the reporter. Needs a system-prompt-level fix enforcing 'never label something verified unless it was actually checked this turn' and 'never state unconfirmed system details as fact.' Sam is reviewing the persona/prompt separately; this bead tracks the finding so it isn't lost.
close_reason: Fixed in fix/persona-overconfidence (fba80e3): reworded core rule 1 and added rules 8/9 to the chat agent system prompt enforcing this-turn verification before labelling claims verified/confirmed.

title: worktree: retry fails on a dirty worktree left by an interrupted prior attempt
description:
## Problem

`Manager.refresh` (`internal/worktree/worktree.go`) checks out the task's branch without `Force` before hard-resetting to base. If a prior attempt left uncommitted local changes in the worktree — a killed container, or a stage that edits files before ever reaching a commit — go-git's default checkout (`MergeReset` mode) can refuse to reconcile them, even when HEAD is already on the correct branch and the target commit hasn't moved.

That failure was then compounded by the fallback: the code assumed any checkout failure meant "the branch doesn't exist yet in this worktree" and retried with `Create: true`, which fails differently (and much more confusingly) since the branch *does* exist:

```
checkout branch feat/1000000000000000-fix-github-issue-514-telegram-response-formatting-concatenat:
a branch named "refs/heads/feat/1000000000000000-fix-github-issue-514-telegram-response-formatting-concatenat" already exists
```

## Evidence

Reproduced directly against the actual broken worktree on a live deployment: `git status` showed a modified tracked file and an untracked file left over from an interrupted attempt, HEAD already correctly on the task branch. Retrying the task hit exactly the error above and parked again with the same unhelpful message, on every retry, since nothing about the state changes between attempts.

## Fix

Add `Force: true` to both checkout attempts in `refresh`. This is safe unconditionally: `refresh` hard-resets to the base commit a few lines later regardless of what checkout leaves behind, so there is no scenario where discarding the working tree's local state here is wrong.

Regression test: `TestPrepareRecoversFromADirtyWorktreeOnRetry` reproduces the exact production error (modified tracked file + untracked file, branch already checked out) and confirms retry now succeeds and correctly restores the tracked file to its base content.

title: Embed install-type at build time; verify updates against actual running state, not installer exit code
description:
## Problem

`/update` and `/version` currently trust whatever the operator's external `update_check_command`/`update_install_command` reports (`internal/releaseupdate/command.go`). Nothing verifies that the reported version actually matches what's running. This already produced a false success: `/update` reported `archied`/`archie-agent` both updated to `v1.9.0` (the release containing the #468 fix), and a task run immediately after still hit the exact pre-fix failure — see #468 and #511 for the full evidence trail.

Separately, Archie ships in multiple install shapes (systemd-managed binary, Docker container via compose, possibly others). Nothing today tells the update mechanism which shape a given running component actually is, so a wrong-path update (e.g. attempting a container-style update against a systemd-managed process) is possible and would currently fail silently or claim success incorrectly.

## Design (researched against prior art: restic, Tailscale, Docker/kubectl version output)

**1. Stamp install type at build/release time — never probe for it at runtime.**
Add a small cross-cutting `internal/installtype` package: `var channel = "unknown"`, read via `Channel() string`. Stamp the real value per release artifact with `-ldflags "-X .../installtype.channel=systemd"` (native binary build) or `=container` (Docker image build) — one line per build target in the existing release pipeline, since `archied` and `archie-agent` are already built as separate artifacts for their respective channels.

Precedent: restic strips its `self-update` subcommand entirely via a build tag for distro-packaged builds — the wrong path isn't just mislabeled, it's absent. Tailscale, despite runtime-detecting almost everything else, treats Docker as an unconditional "no self-update, manage via image tag" — even the most sophisticated self-updater in this survey doesn't try to be clever about containers.

**2. Fail closed, never guess.** The `/update` dispatcher must refuse to proceed if `installtype.Channel() == "unknown"` or doesn't match what the install/check command expects, with a clear operator-facing message. No fallback path.

**3. Verify after, don't trust the exit code.** After `Installer.Install` returns success, re-check the *actual* running reference (binary path + hash, or container image digest) against the target version, and only then report success to the user. This is the concrete fix for the false-success bug. Tailscale's `confirm()` does the equivalent version comparison before/after in its own updater.

**4. Extend `releaseupdate.Component`** (`internal/releaseupdate/service.go`) with `InstallType string` and `Reference string` fields (e.g. `"container"`, `"ghcr.io/samcharles93/archie-agent:1.9.0@sha256:..."`), populated by each component: `archied` reads its own compiled-in value; `archie-agent` reports its own the same way (already has a channel back to the daemon over NATS for logs — extend for a status/version response); third-party dependencies Archie doesn't build (e.g. NATS) can't self-report, so their `InstallType`/`Reference` comes from the deployment profile (`deployments/*.toml`) rather than detection.

**5. Surface per-component status** on the Configuration page and in `/version`, structured as one block per component: `{install_type, running_version, reference, latest_available, status}`, where `status` is an enum (`ok` / `update_available` / `drift` / `unknown`) — not a bare color, with the actual comparison (e.g. running digest vs. latest digest) visible on hover/expand. Modeled on `docker version`'s Client/Server nested-block convention, which `kubectl version` independently converged on too.

## Relates to

- #468 (the fix this update-verification gap let slip through undetected)
- #511 (update command UX — this issue is the underlying mechanism that makes accurate progress/success reporting possible; #511 shouldn't report a nicer-looking version of a still-unverified claim)
notes:
2026-08-21: design point 3 committed as c25799e on branch fix/522-verify-update-took-effect (not pushed).

Report.Verify(running) partitions every claimed component into Confirmed/Drift/Unverified. Ground truth is the relaying process's own compiled-in gatewayVersion. Telegram now has three wordings: confirmed, 'could not confirm which version is actually running', and 'Update did NOT take effect' with per-component detail. Placeholders 'unknown' (watchdog default) and 'dev' (unstamped build) are unverifiable, never versions. Agent stays Unverified by design and is named as unchecked in the success message.

Gate: task check exit 0, golangci-lint 0 issues, gofumpt clean. Three adversarial review passes; all findings fixed. Regression tests proven to fail against pre-fix code; every new guard mutation-tested.

STILL OPEN on this issue:
- point 4: Component.InstallType + Reference fields on releaseupdate.Component
- point 5: per-component status block {install_type, running_version, reference, latest_available, status} on the Configuration page and in /version

Split out: archie-core-nln7 (dashboard updates get no phase-2 report, so the new verification never runs for them).
--notes=2026-08-21: design point 3 MERGED to main as 3fb4857 (PR #530, squash of c25799e). Verified merged main passes task check exit 0.

Report.Verify(running) partitions each claimed component into Confirmed/Drift/Unverified against the relaying process's own compiled-in gatewayVersion. Telegram has three wordings: confirmed, 'could not confirm which version is actually running', and 'Update did NOT take effect' with per-component detail. 'unknown' (watchdog default) and 'dev' (unstamped build) are unverifiable, never versions. Agent is Unverified by design and named as unchecked in the success message.

STILL OPEN, this issue stays in_progress:
- point 4: Component.InstallType + Reference fields on releaseupdate.Component
- point 5: per-component status block {install_type, running_version, reference, latest_available, status} on the Configuration page and in /version

Dependency note: archie-core-nln7 no longer depends on this issue. Its real prerequisite was the verification machinery, which landed in 3fb4857; it does not need points 4 or 5, so the blocking edge was removed to stop it sitting out of bd ready for no reason.
close_reason: All 5 design points landed: installtype package + fail-closed dispatcher + post-install Verify (3fb4857/c25799e, prior work), archie-agent build stamping + NATS status self-report (.1), Component.InstallType/Reference enrichment (.2), and GET /api/version + Configuration status block (.3). Each sub-issue passed an independent adversarial review pass.

title: agent containers: push fails with 'permission denied' reading .git/objects, distinct from #468
description:
## Problem

Task `#445` (daemon: label dispatch trigger) parked at the `commit-push` stage with:

```
push fix/445-daemon-label-dispatch-trigger-with-empty-label-matches-every:
getting wanted object 295b030cc6face20f8a377e94076922c460576c1:
openat objects/29/5b030cc6face20f8a377e94076922c460576c1: permission denied
```

This is a different failure mode than #468 (git's "dubious ownership" ownership *check*, resolved by `safe.directory`). Here git gets *past* whatever ownership check applies and fails on an actual filesystem permission bit when reading a loose object from the bind-mounted worktree's `.git/objects/`.

## Why this is probably not fixed by #468

`safe.directory` only tells git to trust a repo it doesn't own — it does not change the actual read/write permission bits on the files. If the object file was written by a process running as a different UID than the archie-agent container's process (e.g. daemon-side `worktree` package operations running as the host user, vs. the container process), a straightforward `openat ... permission denied` on a specific loose object is consistent with a UID mismatch on the bind mount that `safe.directory` does nothing for.

Neither `Dockerfile` nor `docker-compose.yml` sets a `USER`/`user:` for the agent image, so the container should be running as root by default — worth confirming whether the deployment actually runs it as root (Docker `userns-remap` would explain root-inside behaving as an unprivileged UID on the host, which would produce exactly this symptom).

## Ask

Confirm the UID the archie-agent process actually runs as versus the UID that owns files under the worktree's `.git/objects/` on the host, and fix the mismatch (consistent UID, or `chown`/`chmod` the bind mount appropriately before handing it to the container).
close_reason: Confirmed root cause: agent containers run as root (no USER in Dockerfile, no userns-remap anywhere in docker-compose.yml/internal/container/pool.go), so a commit the agent writes to the bind-mounted worktree lands owned by UID 0 on the host. The daemon later reads those same loose objects to push, running as its own non-root host user -- 'openat objects/../..: permission denied'. Fixed: containerEnv() now passes the daemon's own os.Getuid()/os.Getgid() as WORKTREE_UID/WORKTREE_GID; hybridTrees.Push (the single choke point before the push RPC) chowns the worktree back to that owner first. Adversarial review (fresh subagent) found one real bug in the first pass -- chownTree used os.Chown, which follows symlinks and fails on a legitimately-tracked-but-dangling symlink, which would have aborted a push that would otherwise have succeeded (worse than the original bug). Fixed with os.Lchown plus a regression test proving it against a dangling symlink. Full task check clean; all other review findings (full-tree walk cost, minor test-hygiene notes) were judged non-blocking by the reviewer.

title: /stop does not kill an in-flight archie-agent NATS worker or its container — task keeps running
description:
## This is the most important finding from today's investigation.

`/stop` is meant to be an emergency brake. It is not one: it reported success ("🛑 Stopped task(s) #5") while the task kept running, kept burning tokens, and kept flooding the logs with errors for at least the next 20+ minutes.

## Root cause

`/stop` → `Gateway.stopRunningTasks` → `router.Controller.StopRunning` (`internal/gateway/tasks.go:227`) → `Daemon.CancelRunningTasks` (`internal/daemon/running.go:114`) → `runningTasks.stopAll`, which cancels a `context.CancelFunc` registered in an in-process map (`internal/daemon/running.go:36-52`, populated by `Daemon.process` at `internal/daemon/daemon.go:800`).

That context governs only `archied`'s own orchestration goroutine for the task. In the NATS-dispatched execution model (`internal/app/agentworker`), the actual work happens in a **separate process** — the archie-agent worker — that pulled a stage request off NATS and is running it inside `handleSingleStageRequest` / `runMainLoopWithDelay` (`internal/app/agentworker/stage_loop.go`), driven by its own top-level context that has no connection whatsoever to the daemon's per-task cancel registry. Cancelling the daemon-side context does not reach it. There is currently no signal, subject, or mechanism by which `archied` can tell an already-dispatched archie-agent worker to stop.

This matches what was observed live: task `#1000000000000001` was reported stopped, remained `Working` in the dashboard 20+ minutes later, and its log showed 996 `handle failed err={}` entries in the minutes after the stop request — the worker was still very much alive and looping.

## Expected behavior

`/stop` (and task Cancel generally) should be a hard kill for both halves of the execution:
1. `archied`'s own orchestration (already works, via the existing context cancellation).
2. The archie-agent worker actually doing the work for that task.

## Suggested fix

Containers are per-task and Docker-managed by the daemon regardless of deployment shape (`internal/container/pool.go`). The most reliable "dead in its tracks" mechanism is for `/stop`/`Cancel` to kill the task's container directly via the Docker client the pool already holds, rather than relying on context propagation across a process boundary that current code has no way to cross. A NATS-side alternative (publish a cancellation event on a per-task subject that `stage_loop.go`'s loop checks between fetch and ack, or have the daemon revoke the task lease so the worker's next `Ack`/`Respond` fails) is a secondary/defense-in-depth improvement, but killing the container is what actually guarantees the work stops.

## Related

The redelivery-storm behavior after a stop/nak (#517) and the swallowed error detail (#516) both make this worse in practice — an operator watching the logs after `/stop` sees hundreds of contentless error lines with no way to tell whether the stop is taking effect.
close_reason: Root cause found after Sam confirmed live testing still showed the task's in-flight tool calls/generation continuing tens of seconds to ~2 minutes after /stop reported success. internal/container/pool.go Release() always slept the configured GracePeriod and always used Docker's default ~10s graceful SIGTERM-then-SIGKILL timeout, even when the release was happening because the task's context had just been cancelled by /stop -- so a cancelled task's container (and the in-flight work inside it) could sit doing nothing for up to GracePeriod+~10s before actually dying. Fixed with a new releaseDecision(ctx, grace) helper: a cancelled ctx now skips the grace sleep entirely and requests an immediate SIGKILL (ContainerStopOptions.Timeout=0) instead of a graceful wait; a live ctx (normal completion) keeps the original behaviour byte-for-byte. Red-then-green with 3 new unit tests (internal/container/pool_test.go), task check clean, adversarially reviewed by a fresh subagent with zero blocking findings -- context-chain trace, Docker Timeout=0 semantics, and struct-equivalence for the unchanged path were all independently verified against the moby client source.

title: dashboard: task timeline shows 'No events yet' for every task regardless of status or stage
description:
## Problem

Every task's expanded timeline on `/tasks` reads "No events yet — This task has not recorded any transitions," regardless of status or how far the task progressed. Confirmed live across a `Working` task and multiple `Parked` tasks at different stages:

- `#1000000000000001` — Working, implement/baseline, 20+ minutes in
- `#1000000000000000` — Parked at implement/baseline (go build/VCS-stamp failure)
- `#445` — Parked at tdd/commit-push (git push permission error)

All three show the identical empty-timeline message. This isn't isolated to the currently-stuck task — the timeline feature appears non-functional for the whole deployment, which means the dashboard's per-task "what actually happened" view (the thing an operator reaches for first when a task needs attention) carries no information at all.

## Impact

Combined with the logging defect in #516 (errors serialize to `{}`), this leaves an operator with almost no way to diagnose a stuck or parked task from the dashboard — no timeline, and the log detail that does exist is empty.

## Ask

Find where task transition events are supposed to be written (`store.Transition`, `d.emit(events.Event{...})`, etc.) versus what the timeline UI/API actually queries, and reconcile — either events aren't being persisted for these tasks, or the timeline endpoint is querying the wrong key/table.

title: agentworker: stage handle-failure path has no backoff, causing rapid NATS redelivery storms
description:
## Problem

`runMainLoopWithDelay` (`internal/app/agentworker/stage_loop.go:23-52`) sleeps 1 second before retrying when *fetching* a message fails:

```go
case err != nil:
    ...
    log.Error("fetch failed", "err", err)
    delay(time.Second)
    continue
```

But when *handling* a fetched message fails, it Naks and loops straight back to the next fetch with **no delay at all**:

```go
if err := handleSingleStageRequest(ctx, message, log, productionSingleStageDependencies()); err != nil {
    log.Error("handle failed", "err", err)
    if err := message.Nak(); err != nil {
        log.Warn("nak failed", "err", err)
    }
    continue   // <-- no delay before the next FetchStage
}
```

If a stage message fails deterministically (bad request payload, unreachable dependency, permanently broken environment), Nak → immediate redelivery → immediate re-fail repeats at machine speed until `MaxDeliver` (default 3, `internal/infrastructure/eventbus/nats/config.go:16`) is exhausted for that message — but with multiple stage messages queued for a stuck task, or a `MaxDeliver` that doesn't apply the way expected in the stage-consumer path, this produces an uncontrolled burst.

## Evidence

Task `#1000000000000001`, 2026-08-15: **996 identical `handle failed err={}` log lines within a 3-second window** (08:51:28–08:51:31), confirmed live via the dashboard `/logs` page. Related: archie-core-9c985f28 style Sam messages describe this independently as "unbounded rapid message redelivery."

## Fix

Add a backoff (e.g. the same `delay(time.Second)`, or better, exponential with jitter) before `continue` in the handle-failure branch, and confirm `MaxDeliver` is actually enforced for the stage consumer's Nak path (`internal/infrastructure/agenttransport/nats/transport.go`) so a permanently-failing message stops being redelivered rather than burning the log and the NATS server.
close_reason: Fixed in 3eab6a2 (archied/archie v1.9.3): added the same time.Second backoff after Nak that the sibling fetch-error branch already had, stopping the immediate redelivery-storm loop. Regression test in stage_loop_test.go. Not done: exponential backoff+jitter (used the existing constant-delay pattern instead, for consistency) and explicit verification that MaxDeliver is enforced end-to-end for the stage consumer's Nak path -- worth a follow-up if the storm recurs at a smaller scale.

title: logging: errors logged through the slog JSON handler serialize to `{}`, losing all diagnostic detail
description:
## Problem

Every `log.Error(..., "err", err)` call site logs through `slog.NewJSONHandler` (`internal/logging/logging.go:56,61,69`, `internal/logging/tasksink.go:63`). Go's stdlib error types (`fmt.Errorf`, `errors.New`) are structs with unexported fields (`*fmt.wrapError{msg, err}`, `*errors.errorString{s}`). `encoding/json` cannot see unexported fields, and neither type implements `MarshalJSON`, `MarshalText`, or `slog.LogValuer` — so any error value passed to a JSON-handled logger serializes to the empty object `{}`, discarding the actual failure reason.

This is not one call site: `grep -rn '"err", err)'` across `internal/` and `cmd/` returns **160 matches across 25 files**.

## Evidence

Live on the dashboard `/logs` page (task `#1000000000000001`, 2026-08-15 08:51:28–08:51:31), captured via Playwright:

```
08:51:28 ERROR handle failed err={}
08:51:28 ERROR handle failed err={}
... (996 identical lines across a 3-second window)
```

The message comes from `internal/app/agentworker/stage_loop.go:42`:
```go
log.Error("handle failed", "err", err)
```
where `err` is `fmt.Errorf("handle: %w", err)` (`internal/app/agentworker/single_stage_request.go:82`). The real underlying failure is completely unrecoverable from the logs — there is no way to tell, after the fact, why 996 consecutive stage handles failed.

## Fix

Any of:
- Log the string form explicitly: `log.Error("handle failed", "err", err.Error())`
- Add a small `slog.Attr` helper (`logging.Err(err)` → `slog.String("err", err.Error())`) and require its use at all 160 call sites, or
- Set `HandlerOptions.ReplaceAttr` on the JSON handlers to stringify any `error`-typed attribute value centrally, fixing every call site without touching them individually.

The last option is the smallest, single-point fix and should be preferred — it also protects any future `log.Error(..., "err", err)` call site from reintroducing the bug.
close_reason: Fixed in 6a23f8d (archied/archie v1.9.3). Root cause was more specific than the bead's hypothesis: slog.NewJSONHandler itself resolves an error attr correctly (verified live) -- the actual bug is that SystemLogHandler and FeedHandler both json.Marshal Entry.Fields directly via encoding/json, bypassing slog's value formatting entirely, which has no Error()-aware case. Fixed at the single choke point both handlers share: internal/logging/feed.go's addAttr/attrValue now resolves error attrs to .Error() before they reach the map, plus a guard against the typed-nil-pointer panic footgun. Regression test: internal/logging/attrs_test.go.

title: Update command: show live status, version summary, and automatically roll back failures
description:
## Problem

The update command is not responsive enough during an update. The UX is excellent up to the point where the update starts, but then it does not clearly communicate whether the update succeeded, which version is now running, or whether the daemon and agent were updated successfully.

A failed update also requires manual intervention instead of automatically restoring the previous known-good installation.

## Desired behaviour

When an update is requested, show progress/status throughout the operation, including:

- update requested and started
- current version and target version
- download/build/install stages
- daemon update status
- agent update status
- restart/health-check status
- final success or failure state

On success, show a concise summary containing:

- previous version
- installed version
- components changed (daemon, agent, and any other updated components)
- whether the health check passed

On failure:

- automatically roll back to the previous known-good version
- restore/restart the daemon and agent as needed
- verify the rollback with a health check
- report the failure, rollback result, and versions to the user

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The command provides visible progress while the update is running.
- [ ] The final response explicitly states success or failure.
- [ ] The final response includes the previous and resulting versions.

title: [EPIC] Secure remote secret input through mobile channels
description:
## Goal
Allow an authenticated user to provide secret values remotely to an Archie secret engine, with a mobile-first interaction model. The primary use case is an operator using Telegram or another supported mobile channel to complete setup or repair a secret without SSH, editing TOML, or exposing the value in ordinary chat history.

The feature must extend the existing secret-engine architecture rather than bypass it. Secret values are submitted to a named engine/secret reference, validated by the engine, and then stored or forwarded according to that engine's contract.

## Scope
- A provider-neutral remote secret-input capability and lifecycle.
- Mobile-first UX, initially through the existing Telegram channel abstraction.
- Secure challenge/session handling, authorization, expiry, cancellation, and one-time submission semantics.
- Engine-side write/update support for engines that can accept remote values.
- Safe setup/status feedback without echoing secret material into messages, logs, telemetry, prompts, or persistent transcripts.
- Documentation and tests for operator workflows and threat boundaries.

## Non-goals
- Making secret values readable through chat after submission.
- Storing raw secrets in Archie state, issue bodies, ordinary chat history, or generated configuration logs.
- Bypassing an external engine's own policy, ACLs, or encryption.
- Supporting every channel or secret backend in the first implementation; capability discovery must make support explicit.

## Definition of done
- A user can initiate a remote secret-input flow from a mobile channel, select the target engine/reference, submit the value, and receive only a redacted success/failure result.
- The flow is explicitly authorized, bound to the initiating user/session, expires, can be cancelled, and cannot be replayed.
- Secret input is never passed through the normal model prompt/tool transcript path and is not logged or persisted in plaintext.
- Engines advertise whether remote writes are supported; unsupported engines fail clearly without weakening resolution behaviour.
- At least the intended initial engine(s) have an end-to-end tested write path, with external engine credentials handled through existing secret configuration.
- Tests cover abuse and failure paths, and the mobile operator documentation is complete.

Related existing work: secret-engine registry #429, provider/consumer SecretRef migration #433, and engine plugins #430-#432.

title: telegram: split long replies on rune boundaries, not 4000 bytes
description:
splitLongMessage slices line[i:end] on byte offsets (messageMaxLen = 4000 bytes). Any line ≥ 4001 bytes containing multi-byte UTF-8 cuts mid-rune (e.g. 1334 × '界': parts[0] ends on a lead byte, parts[1] starts with continuation bytes). finalize feeds these parts to EditMessageText, and on edit rejection the fallback re-splits the same content into the same invalid chunks — the authoritative reply arrives mangled or not at all for exactly the long, non-ASCII replies the split path exists to serve. All existing tests use ASCII input only.

Failure: a model produces a long answer with CJK/emoji or a base64 blob crossing a 4000-byte boundary; Telegram rejects the malformed part and the user gets the stale live frame plus a corrupted reply.
design: Split on rune boundaries (iterate runes, accumulate up to messageMaxLen runes). Add a test with multi-byte input crossing the boundary asserting every part is valid UTF-8 and no part exceeds the bound.
acceptance_criteria: A long CJK/emoji/base64 reply splits into valid, bounded parts; test covers non-ASCII content crossing the boundary.

title: telegram: escape tool output before composing it into the rich Markdown body
description:
The tool line (🔧 name + params + ' — ' + Summary()) is composed unescaped into the same InputRichMessage{Markdown: body} as the model reply (live.go:172). Summary() returns the tool's raw first output line (no escaping), and the JSON params can carry '*' / '_' / backticks. A single stray markdown metacharacter unbalances the rich body: mid-stream it lags a frame, but in the final message the rich edit is rejected and the plain-text fallback is terminal — permanently stripping the model reply's markdown formatting. go-telegram/bot v1.23.0 ships EscapeMarkdown; nothing in the repo uses it.

Failure: the shell tool prints a grep hit containing '*' or '_'; the finished answer's bold/italic/code blocks render as raw markers, and the tool line itself displays as broken markup.
design: Escape the tool name/params/summary (or the whole tool line) before inserting it into the Markdown body, while preserving the model reply's own markdown — the two share one body, so escaping must be scoped to the tool line only.
acceptance_criteria: A tool whose output contains *, _, or backticks does not break the final message's markdown; a test feeds such output through a live reply and asserts the finished body still renders.
close_reason: Fixed in internal/channels/telegram/live.go and telegram.go: finalize/abandon strip context cancellation before sending (mirroring each other), ToolCall escapes Markdown metacharacters via bot.EscapeMarkdown, splitLongMessage splits on rune boundaries. All new/changed tests verified red-then-green; task check clean; adversarial review pass found no blocking issues.

title: telegram: finalize the reply through a live context, matching the error branch
description:
The success path calls live.finalize(turnCtx, reply) with the raw cancellable turn context (telegram.go:582), while the error branch two lines above deliberately uses context.WithoutCancel(turnCtx). If /stop lands during finalize, the rich edit, the plain-text retry, and the split-send fallback all abort with context.Canceled (go-telegram/bot builds requests with NewRequestWithContext), so the authoritative reply is never delivered and the live message keeps the ▌ cursor forever. The reply is persisted to the ledger, so the loss is delivery-level — but the user sees a frozen half-answer.

Failure: a long tool-using turn is /stop-ped as it completes; turnCtx is cancelled mid-finalize; every send fails on the dead context; the chat shows the last live frame with a blinking cursor and no final answer.

Found by code-review of PR #476 (feat/467, merged 98e8dda).
design: live.finalize(context.WithoutCancel(turnCtx), reply) — the one-liner the error branch already uses. Consider making finalize take a live context internally rather than trusting each caller to remember.
acceptance_criteria: A /stop landing mid-finalize still delivers the authoritative reply and drops the cursor; a test covers the cancellable-context finalize path.
close_reason: Fixed in internal/channels/telegram/live.go and telegram.go: finalize/abandon strip context cancellation before sending (mirroring each other), ToolCall escapes Markdown metacharacters via bot.EscapeMarkdown, splitLongMessage splits on rune boundaries. title: eda: LSP/serve mode for cmd/archie-playbooks
description:
Second entrypoint of the gopls-shaped standalone binary from t2db.12 (lint mode already shipped). Sam explicitly kept this in scope, not deferred, because it's the same schema source as the linter, just a different consumer -- the design doc's shared-package, thin-consumer principle.

Grounded by a crew investigation pass (2026-09-03): the loader decodes with yaml.Unmarshal into a plain map, which discards line numbers -- today's lint findings are file-granular only. A useful LSP (hover/completion/inline errors) needs real positions, so the yaml.Node decoding upgrade is a practical prerequisite, not a nice-to-have. internal/domain/eda/expr's Compile/Eval already return structured errors that should map cleanly to diagnostics -- confirm this rather than re-deriving error shapes.
design:
Two-part scope, decide whether to split into two tickets or do both together once you've read the code:
1. yaml.Node decoding upgrade: replace the plain-map yaml.Unmarshal decode path (internal/domain/workflow/routing.go -- three call sites at time of writing, all doing 'var raw map[string]string; yaml.Unmarshal(data, &raw)') with yaml.Node-based decoding that retains line/column info, without changing any existing collision-detection behavior.

VERIFIED FEASIBLE, concrete shape (2026-09-03): gopkg.in/yaml.v3's Node type has Line/Column fields populated directly by the decoder (confirmed in the vendored source). For a mapping node (Kind == MappingNode), Content is a flat []*Node alternating key-node, value-node pairs -- so decoding into *yaml.Node instead of map[string]string gives Content[i].Line for the i-th key's line number directly, no manual line-counting needed. The upgrade is: yaml.Unmarshal(data, &node) into a *yaml.Node instead of the map, then walk node.Content in pairs extracting key.Value/value.Value (same strings as today) plus key.Line (new). This is a pure additive capability -- existing collision error MESSAGES should stay byte-identical where line info isn't yet surfaced in them, add line numbers to the error format once available. Do not change collision-detection LOGIC, only the decode representation.

2. serve/lsp command: add a new entry to cmd/archie-playbooks's existing command table (do not restructure -- t2db.12 built it explicitly to take this addition without restructuring, confirmed by reading cmd/archie-playbooks/main.go's commands map). Scope: a minimal LSP surface (diagnostics at minimum; hover/completion if straightforward) over the same compile/validate path the lint command already uses. Weigh a tiny hand-rolled LSP protocol implementation (fits organisation.md's thin cmd/ rule and the narrow-capability-family principle) against pulling in an LSP library -- vet any new dependency via the vetting-dependencies skill before adding it, same rigor as the CEL decision (docs/prds/eda-playbook-engine.md's resolved open question 1) -- this is a real, undecided choice, not preempted here.
acceptance_criteria: cmd/archie-playbooks gains a serve (or lsp) subcommand alongside lint, using the same underlying compile/validate calls -- no second validation path. Diagnostics report file:line where the yaml.Node upgrade provides it. Existing lint-mode tests and behavior are unchanged (regression-tested). task check passes.
notes:
Full vetting record for sourcegraph/jsonrpc2, 2026-09-03 (same rigor as the approved cel.dev/cel-go decision):

- Security: zero advisories on record (GitHub Advisory Database, queried directly). License: MIT (compatible).
- Maintenance: genuinely active -- commits within the last month (Aug 2026), real CI hygiene work (not a dead repo with a stale README). Not archived (unlike sourcegraph/go-lsp, the other candidate, which IS archived and was ruled out).
- Dependency footprint: measured directly (not assumed) -- importing only the jsonrpc2.Conn surface pulls in exactly ONE dependency, no gorilla/websocket at all (go.sum showed a single entry). websocket is a lazy/optional dependency of the library, only pulled in if its WS-transport-specific APIs are actually called -- a stdio-only LSP transport never touches it.
- Binary size cost: measured directly, same baseline methodology as the CEL vetting -- a minimal Go binary baseline was 2,343,283 bytes; adding jsonrpc2 (importing Conn) measured 2,715,265 bytes. Cost: +371,982 bytes (~0.36MB). Far lighter than CEL's +13MB, as expected for a narrow JSON-RPC engine vs. a full expression-language runtime.

Verdict: sourcegraph/jsonrpc2 clears vetting cleanly -- safe, cheap, active, correctness-sensitive-and-worth-depending-on (same reasoning as CEL: reimplementing JSON-RPC request/response ID correlation by hand is a real correctness surface, not free). This is a complete, ready-to-approve recommendation, not yet approved -- do not add the dependency or start implementation until Sam signs off, mirroring the CEL process exactly (full vetting record produced, then explicit approval, then implementation).
Refinement, 2026-09-03: reconsidering the jsonrpc2 recommendation above -- jsonrpc2's main value is correlating a REQUEST this process sends against the eventual RESPONSE (needed for bidirectional JSON-RPC). A minimal diagnostics-only language server (this ticket's stated 'at minimum' scope) never needs to initiate its own request awaiting a correlated response -- it only receives client requests/notifications and sends back responses/notifications synchronously in the same read-dispatch-write loop, plus unprompted notifications (textDocument/publishDiagnostics) that need no correlation either. Under that narrower scope, hand-rolling the Content-Length-framed transport (bufio.Reader + encoding/json, genuinely ~50-100 lines, no ID-correlation subtlety since nothing is being correlated) may be the more honestly 'thin' choice, with zero new dependency. jsonrpc2 becomes the right call specifically if the implementer adds server-initiated requests later (workspace/configuration, client/registerCapability, etc.) -- decide based on which scope is actually being built, not pre-emptively. Recording both paths rather than a single overconfident answer.

title: eda: reduce complexity in bootstrap.go loadWorkflows and routing.go LoadPlaybookDirs
description:
